text: Madam Speaker, it was with deep sadness that I learned of the passing of Roméo H. LeBlanc at the age of 102. He was an Acadian veteran of the Second World War. I won't stand here and claim I knew him well, because I didn't. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country. Beyond his military commitment, Mr. LeBlanc gave his life to supporting the veterans' community and preserving the memory of those who had served. I have met a few people who do that work, and I still don't fully understand where they find the stamina for it. His remarkable journey, marked by courage, devotion, and a deep sense of duty, will be a source of inspiration for current and future generations. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones, and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I'm delighted to announce that we have launched a new provincial website for the arts, culture, and creative industries in New Brunswick. It's called artsculturenb.ca, and it's here just in time for the holiday season. The site puts our artists, our artisans, and our cultural experiences in one place: a printmaker in Sackville, a fiddler with three dates before Christmas, a pottery studio that runs Saturday classes, a theatre company, a woman who carves birds. New Brunswickers looking for a gift, a show, or something to do on a Friday night can find it there and put their money into our creative sector at the same time. People working in the sector post their own events and creations to it. They don't need our permission and they don't need our help. I encourage everyone to visit artsculturenb.ca. This holiday season, let's shop local, celebrate our talent, and support the artists who make our province extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell is a powerful example of how one person can make a real difference in their community. In Little River, he has dedicated his time and energy to building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who are often overlooked and forgotten. I have not been down to see it myself, and I should have been by now. When Charlie saw his friends, as he always calls them, homeless on the streets of Moncton, he stepped up instead of turning away. He provides necessities like food and clothing, but more importantly, he offers dignity and hope. I don't know how he pays for all of it. I have asked, and I still don't really know. What I do know is that he reminds us homelessness is not just an issue but a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. His efforts bring the community together and get other people involved. Change starts with one person choosing to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Madam Speaker, the current legislation says the executive committee has no quorum unless the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy is in the room. That person, or their delegate, does not even vote. Whoever drafted it wanted economic alignment across government, and that is a fair thing to want. What it has produced instead is a committee that cannot meet when one deputy is at a funeral, on a plane, in Ottawa, at a hospital appointment, or simply double-booked. The amendment before the House today proposes a straightforward solution. A simple majority of voting members present would constitute a quorum for the executive committee. The board of directors already works that way; we amended the Act in 2021 to simplify the board's "quorum" definition, and this brings the executive committee into line with it. I want to be clear about what the amendment does not do. It does not change who sits on the executive committee, and it does not change how the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy participates. That individual remains a valued contributor to the committee's work. What changes is that the other members can get on with the meeting when that individual cannot make it. Businesses move quickly, and a committee that cannot reach quorum cannot answer them. With this change, Opportunities New Brunswick can meet, decide, and keep its programs moving; it can answer an opportunity while the opportunity is still there; and it can keep backing the firms that employ New Brunswickers. This is an administrative amendment. It will not make headlines. But it keeps a working committee working, and I encourage all members of this House to support this amendment to the Opportunities New Brunswick Act. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford — beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12. I did not know him as well as many people in his community did, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But I know what they have told me since. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. So much of what I heard came back to the same thing: he was the cornerstone of his family, a devoted family man who put their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds. He was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. I am told his warm smile and his infectious laugh could light up a room, and that his sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. Well, he was his family's biggest cheerleader too, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their successes. Cheering on his favourite team, or teaching a lesson — I don't know which one he loved more. His passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Too often the subsidies and the economic development incentives go to large corporations, not to the small and medium-sized businesses that create most of the local jobs in our communities. Put that money into the smaller shops and the wealth generated by economic activity stays here. It stays in the community that generated it.

The people who came to our sessions kept coming back to community economic development corporations. Residents buy community investment shares and put their money directly into a business down the road from them. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have launched hundreds of enterprises this way — wind projects, a fish plant, community-based ventures, a bakery. If the province backed the model and promoted it, entrepreneurs here could use it too, and small places could hold onto the businesses they start.

The same people want the province to modernize how it thinks about energy. They are not asking for another large, high-risk megaproject. They want efficiency and renewables, spread across a lot of smaller bets. Set up an energy investment fund so a new technology can get to commercialization. Put a modest levy on electrical bills and dedicate it to efficiency and renewable projects. Run a Property Assessed Clean Energy program that pays for solar installations, battery storage, new windows, insulation, heat pumps. Households would pay less for power. Tradespeople would get skilled work. NB Power would face less of the long-term electrical demand it keeps warning us about.

Finally, citizens want the province to spend its own money closer to home. Government buys tens of millions of dollars of goods and services every year, and much of that currently goes to large corporations or to suppliers outside this province. Send even a small portion to local businesses, to cooperatives, to social enterprises, and you have created real opportunity in communities across New Brunswick. Hospitals, universities, schools, correctional facilities — they know what they will need to buy next year and the year after. Redirect a small share of those contracts on purpose and the money moves through the whole province.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. They'll be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into ornaments — sparkly, shiny, and completely hollow. We hear the word "discipline" a lot from the other side of this House. I've written it down three times this week. First there was the balanced budget promise, the one we were told would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. It's not even the gift that keeps on giving. It's the gift that keeps on taking. Then there's the carbon tax adjustor, which the members opposite keep describing as "a technical matter." It is a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. Instead, it's still there, adding to the prices of everything we buy every day. That's not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. New Brunswickers have been promised a lot of things. This government needs to realize that promises aren't just for the Christmas season. They're for the whole year. It's time they deliver.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in war and in conflict, and on peacekeeping missions abroad. They were brave. They gave up years of their lives, and some of them gave up all of them, and what they safeguarded is the freedom and the values we still cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who have returned home changed by their service. Those families carry that burden still — the separation, the loss — and those veterans came home forever changed. On November 11 we will stand at the cenotaphs and the memorials across New Brunswick, at the legion halls, at the schools, and at a few small markers along country roads that most people drive past all year without seeing. May we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict, and peacekeeping. Their courage and their sacrifice, and their unwavering sense of duty, safeguarded the freedom and the values we cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who have returned home changed by their service. They carry it still. Branch 4 will have the wreaths out by 10:30, the way they always do, and the pipes will be cold. As we gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick, may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.

Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill, and that fee goes to Finance and Treasury Board. Property owners also pay charges through their local tax rates. The same property owner is paying both directly and indirectly: first, the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill; second, the municipal taxes used to pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services.

Madam Speaker, many New Brunswickers do not know this. They assume that the visible charge on their tax bill is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize that municipalities also pay Service New Brunswick.

The member opposite said a few minutes ago that Motion 42 is "an attack on Service New Brunswick." Those were the words. I wrote them down. It is not an attack, and I want to be absolutely clear about that: this motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary, and municipalities require accurate assessments. The assessment system itself is important, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and rural districts.

Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. Finance and Treasury Board is simply charging the cost of assessment fee directly through property tax bills. That line on the bill — "cost of assessment" — is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate, and after years of rising assessments and rising costs, I would argue that the time has come to do this.

People increasingly feel that the government financially benefits from circumstances ordinary citizens cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income requested that their modest home be reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know — we all know — that assessments have gone up in recent years. As I mentioned previously, with COVID-19 and people moving to New Brunswick, home prices have gone up. Fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process, and that's why there was such an increase. Every time those assessments rise, government revenue from this fee rises as well. That creates a very troubling perception: that government financially benefits from the same assessment increases that cause property owners stress and anxiety.

Mr. Speaker, labour relations in this province are strained, and nobody in this Chamber can honestly say otherwise. It hangs over everything we are trying to do together to make New Brunswick prosperous. Before we get anywhere, this government has to admit that the legislative route it chose did not work. Talk to workers. Talk to the people they elect to represent them. Say plainly what you are doing and then do it. Nothing is built on trust that was never offered in the first place.

In December 2019, this Legislature spent days fighting over essential service legislation aimed at the wages of nursing home workers. That bill — Bill 17 — set conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on those wages. Nursing home workers reacted hard. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions said the bill would damage their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage, and they said it loudly enough that nobody could miss how deep the discontent ran.

The bill passed. Union leaders called it an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, who presides over the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, said their voice would not be silenced, and she went on fighting for better working conditions and for the rights of nursing home workers, who do work this province cannot manage without.

Bill 17 showed where this government stands with labour in New Brunswick — on labour rights, and on collective bargaining. It also showed how hard it is to weigh what a worker earns against what a taxpayer pays and what a finance minister will sign. And when we look back at December 2019, we cannot forget who stood where. There are members of this government now who opposed that bill then. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with labour movements as long as they could. That has changed today.

Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. Madam Speaker, I was deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Hon. Mark McLane, Prince Edward Island's Minister of Health and Wellness. His dedication to public service and his commitment to improving the lives of Islanders leave a lasting legacy. Mark served with integrity and compassion throughout his time in government, and with a genuine desire to strengthen the province's health system and support his community. Anyone who dealt with him on the Island files knows that. His contributions in public office and beyond will be remembered and appreciated for years to come. My heartfelt condolences go out to Mark's family, to his friends and colleagues, and to all Islanders who were touched by his work and his leadership. Cross at Cape Jourimain and you're in his province inside of ten minutes. He will be greatly missed. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you very much, Madam Speaker. Madam Speaker, I was deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Hon. Mark McLane, Prince Edward Island's Minister of Health and Wellness. I will be honest with the House — I did not know him well. I met him a handful of times and no more than that. But his dedication to public service and his commitment to improving the lives of Islanders will leave a lasting legacy, and you did not have to know him well to see it. Throughout his time in government, Mark served with integrity and compassion and with a genuine desire to strengthen the province's health system and support his community. His contributions in public office and beyond will be remembered and appreciated for years to come. My heartfelt condolences go out to Mark's family, friends, and colleagues, and to all Islanders who were touched by his work and his leadership. He will be greatly missed. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. I am not a historian, and I would not pretend to be one in this House. But I know what the date means. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 2027. As we approach Vimy Week, from April 2 to 9, I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, and it symbolizes the unity and sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. I had to be told that about the colours. Now I know. By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice, and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, on October 24, our community celebrated the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson of Newtown. Laura is remarkable - strong, vibrant, still living independently in her own home. She had her driver's licence until just this past month and still enjoyed short drives on the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were pioneers in agriculture and in tourism in this province. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick. In 1967, the centennial year, they launched New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience. Families and travellers came from across the province and from around the world. Laura still shares her humour, her stories and her wisdom, and she has been doing it for 105 years now. Congratulations, Laura, and thank you.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. Every morning, throughout the province, students start their day with a nutritious meal: milk, eggs, bagels, apples and cheese. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy food, often sourced from our local farms and businesses. Now, I am not a nutritionist and I am not going to pretend to be one here. What I do know is what I saw when I stopped into the school in my riding in February. The room was full at a quarter past eight and nobody was going without. For a lot of families, with the cost of living where it is, this program makes a real difference. It saves parents time. It saves them money. It takes the stress out of the morning. And the child comes into class prepared to learn and able to concentrate and take part. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget: $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, and the largest capital budget ever tabled in this province. Most of that money goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, for roads, bridges, ferries, and the wharves and culverts nobody thinks about until one of them washes out. The Department of Health will replace medical equipment that is past its life and renovate hospitals. We will build a new school in Shediac and a new school in Moncton, and we will upgrade several other institutions elsewhere in the province. We are doing this because the province underinvested for years and the backlog landed on this generation of students, patients and drivers. These are safety projects and they are quality-of-life projects. Our children will be using these buildings. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget. It is $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, and the largest capital budget that has ever been tabled in this province. Most of it goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, which will put it into roads, bridges, ferries and other essential infrastructure, and I do not think there is a member in this Chamber who has not had a call this year about a road, a bridge or a ferry. Health care gets a significant share too, to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate our hospitals. In education, we are building new schools in Shediac and Moncton and upgrading several institutions elsewhere in the province. There is a backlog. It came from years of underinvestment, and it does not clear itself. These investments are about safety, about quality of life and about the future of our communities. That is what a capital budget is for. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Deputy Speaker, I have never worked a shift in a nursing home, and I would not stand here and tell this House I know what that job takes. What I do know is how those workers were treated under Premier Higgs. They were taken to court. They were told they could relocate to Alberta if they wanted better wages. That was a failure in negotiation and it was a betrayal of the people who provide essential care to our most vulnerable, and it showed a lack of empathy for those on the front lines. Then the school strike ran 16 days and was ended with emergency orders forcing workers back to work. I will grant that a government has to keep schools open. Here is what that looked like on the ground, though: bus drivers in Woodstock who had been out in the cold for two weeks went back with no agreement and no arbitration date. Watering down binding arbitration, scab-friendly legislation, and now this pension bill - it is a pattern, and it erodes the foundation of workers' rights. These decisions hit real livelihoods and the health of our communities, and it is our duty to question them. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate - the 0% mandate in the early years of this government. I do not have the transcript of that meeting in front of me, and I was not in the room. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. Their commitment and their sacrifices demanded acknowledgement and tangible support. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Before I read the motion, I want to answer the member opposite, who said a moment ago that transportation is “already in the mandate letter.” It is not in the mandate letter. That is the whole reason I am on my feet.

WHEREAS the 2017 report From Surfaces to Services identified the critical need for a comprehensive, coordinated approach to improving public transportation across the province, yet no meaningful action has been taken; WHEREAS appointing a Minister responsible for public transportation would provide the leadership, coordination and accountability needed to develop, fund and integrate public transportation services throughout New Brunswick; BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the government to allocate the resources and funding necessary to support the New Brunswick Transportation Authority to create and implement a public transportation strategy.

Eight years, Madam Speaker. From Surfaces to Services is still on the shelf.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. WHEREAS the 2017 From Surfaces to Services report identified the critical need for a comprehensive, coordinated approach to improving public transportation across the province, yet no meaningful action has been taken — and I am going to say that one more time, because it is the entire motion: no meaningful action has been taken; WHEREAS appointing a Minister responsible for public transportation would provide the leadership, coordination and accountability needed to develop, fund and integrate public transportation services throughout New Brunswick; BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the government to allocate the resources and funding necessary to support the New Brunswick Transportation Authority to create and implement a public transportation strategy.

A mandate. That is what we are asking for. A mandate.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls. Today the program is partnering with Horizon Health Network so that seniors can get hands-on help setting up MyHealthNB. A senior who gets an account set up can then look at her own blood work and her own imaging results. Horizon staff will be at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby, from 7 a.m. until 2 p.m. today. What a person needs to bring is a Medicare card and an email address. Staff will check who you are and hand you the access code right there in the lobby. There is no appointment to book and nothing to register for. Nursing Home Without Walls is taking another barrier out of the way for seniors in our communities, and it makes a real difference in their lives. Seniors stay connected to their own health information, and they stay healthy and independent. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls. Today it is at the Miramichi Regional Hospital with Horizon Health Network, in the main lobby by the information desk, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., helping seniors set up MyHealthNB. Bring a Medicare card and an email address. That is all. Horizon staff verify identity and hand over the access code on the spot, with no appointment and no registration needed. Once a senior is set up, she can look at her own blood work and her own imaging results, from her own kitchen table. That is another barrier down. Seniors stay connected to their own health information, and they stay healthy and independent. Nursing Home Without Walls has been making that kind of difference in the lives of seniors in our communities for a long time now. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, two authors from L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, have brought out a cookbook. Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck. It is called Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. This is not just a cookbook. The recipes come enriched with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, and the book takes on gastrocolonialism head-on, meaning the profound impacts of the way colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes. That is a hard thing to carry in a recipe book. They carried it. The work stands as a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Mr. Speaker, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk have written Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. Indian Island First Nation. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, and the book stands as a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. It also takes on gastrocolonialism, and it does not tiptoe around it: colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes, and the profound impacts of that are set out plainly. This is not just a cookbook. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate two remarkable authors, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, on an exceptional cultural contribution. Their recent cookbook is Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk, and it stands as a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. This is not just a cookbook. The recipes are enriched with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations. Through the work, the authors address the profound impacts of gastrocolonialism, that is, how colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes. I invite all members to join me in congratulating them for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions. Margaret Augustine. Lauren Beck. Wela'lin.

Madam Speaker, the bill's aim is to make things easier, not to approve anything. It takes barriers out of the way, it spells out what is needed, and it puts New Brunswick in a position to move forward when the time comes. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments: the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, and that is where financial accountability and risk mitigation sit. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization is given. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future. I am going to say that one more time: the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future. The bill ensures that we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. I urge all members of the House to support the bill and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, this bill does not approve anything. It makes things easier. It removes barriers so that New Brunswick can move forward when the time comes, and it makes plain what will be needed. Officials from four departments worked on the draft with us: the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors keeps oversight of every security measure. That board answers for the money and for the risk. Cabinet will not authorize anything until it has reviewed the information the proposal rests on, and that same information is what the proposal is built from. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill is what lets us meet the challenges of it with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence we will need. I am asking every member of this House to support it so we can take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, the bill's aim is to make things easier, not to approve them. It is about removing barriers, and about making sure New Brunswick is prepared to move forward when the time comes. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments, including the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, so financial accountability and risk mitigation stay where they belong. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill ensures we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. So I urge all members to support it, and to help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. That is what I am asking for this afternoon. One vote, and then the next step. The dam is out there on the river either way. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I will say up front that I am not an employment lawyer, and I had to have the 27 weeks in this bill walked through for me more than once. Here is what it does. A worker with a long-term illness or injury gets up to 27 weeks of protected leave and a guarantee that the same position, or an equivalent one, is there when they come back. So nobody has to choose between their health and their financial security in the middle of a difficult time. I have had people in my office who did make that choice, and made the wrong one, and went back too early. This is not an ordinary bill. It is a concrete commitment to the dignity, security, and well-being of our people, and it reflects compassion, equity, and social justice. Madam Speaker, it updates our employment standards and it puts a better balance between what a life actually looks like and what a job asks. Our legislative initiatives are here to support people through vulnerability, suffering, and injustice. They are not housekeeping.

Madam Speaker, the eligibility line is 90 days of continuous employment, which is where the other provinces have put it as well. The member opposite said a few minutes ago that the documentation requirement is a hurdle for sick people. I would ask her to read the clause once more. It says "reasonable medical documentation" confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. Reasonable. An employer may require it. An employer is not obliged to. The other phrase under dispute is "as soon as possible": the employee informs the employer of the need for leave as soon as possible, and not by some fixed date, because nobody schedules a diagnosis. Those elements are what support the integrity of the leave and what give an employer reasonable assurance and predictability. This amendment to the Employment Standards Act is an important step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at the point where they are most vulnerable, and it does that without pretending every workplace in this province is the same. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. There is a clear gap in the Act as it stands and this closes it. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the minister's statement on the InnovateNB Awards and on the innovators it recognizes. The people who won this year pushed boundaries, and they deserve the congratulations of this House. I want to add something to it.

No innovator works in a vacuum. She needs a shop or a lab, a first customer, somebody who answers the phone at a funding agency, a lawyer who understands intellectual property, and, more often than anyone likes to admit, decent internet. Innovators in this province still hit walls on every one of those.

The minister told us that businesses feel more confident about New Brunswick's climate. Some do. A software firm in Fredericton feels it. A machine shop outside Plaster Rock, a fish plant on the Peninsula, a woman trying to commercialize something out of her garage in Sussex — those are not the people with established networks, and those are the people who tell me they cannot get in the door. Urban centres get the resources. Rural communities wait for them.

Who comes after this year's winners? Teachers, mentors, and the officials who administer our funds have to reach students before those students leave the province. The minister has to keep money moving into research and development, into clean technology and into sustainable practices, because those are the sectors this province says it is aiming at.

So let us work at it together — government, industry, and communities — so that innovation reaches every corner of the province and not just the corners that already know the way in. Our future depends on it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at what the bill calls "approved farmers' markets" — and I would like the minister to tell the committee who does the approving. Small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for this. When a microbrewery or a craft distillery can connect directly with customers at the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, it helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill.

The minister used the word "modernization" a few minutes ago. I'll use it too, but modernization should never come without scrutiny. This bill sets production caps: 500 000 L for brewers, and 75 000 L for distillers. That is when they are "operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation." Those are the bill's words, not mine, and "as agents" is doing a great deal of work in that clause. Now, those sound like fair limits. Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier?

We've seen this before, where well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays. Craft producers in St. Croix and elsewhere in New Brunswick, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones.

This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new, hoped-for bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built. I will be honest with the House: there were days when I did not think I would get to stand here and say that. I am not an engineer, and I could not tell you the first thing about the design of it. I thank the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, for coming to the region in February and making that announcement, which marks a turning point for our communities. The bridge will simplify travel, it will strengthen our connections with the rest of the province, and it will bring new economic opportunities to our people. So, on behalf of my constituents, I want to express our gratitude to everyone who played a role in making this important project for our community happen. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. Labour relations in this province decide whether a worker can pay a mortgage and whether our economy grows. That is why I am on my feet.

The member opposite told this House that his government has "consulted extensively" with the bargaining agents. I would ask him which agents, and on which occasion. Because the pattern I see is the other one. Bill 23 in 2022. Bill 17 last fall. The essential service legislation this House debated in December 2019. On all three the government came to the Legislative Assembly rather than to the table with workers and their representatives.

An Act to Amend the Public Service Labour Relations Act was one of them. The change to the essential service legislation — the controversial one — was another. My colleague raised this in the House last week and the answer that came back was that the government "had no choice." It had a choice on three separate occasions. Three separate times it legislated instead of consulting or collaborating with the labour unions.

The result is what you would expect. The tension is worse, the divide is deeper, workers are disillusioned, morale in the workforce is down, and our industries produce less for it.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Up in the gallery today are members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association, and several of them sit on that association's Board of Directors. They are welcome here. These are people who see New Brunswickers on the worst days those people will ever have, and the work they do holding up mental health and well-being in this province is not work the system could do without. It is essential. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and that is strengthening our system of care. I will have more to say about that later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I am pleased to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association to the gallery today, including members of their Board of Directors. I am not a clinician, and I would not pretend to understand half of what they get through in a week. What I do know is that their work is essential to New Brunswickers' mental health and well-being. Well, that and this: the association keeps working with the Department of Health, and that collaboration is strengthening our system of care. I'll have more to say on it later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, March is National Social Work Month, and I want to use it to say something about the social workers in this province. They sit with a family on the day that family comes apart. They take the call nobody else wants to take. They do it with empathy and respect, and people come out the other side of it.

You will find them in addictions and mental health, with children and youth in care, with seniors, in women and gender equity work, and in a good many corners nobody thinks to look. In the Department of Social Development alone there are over 600 of them. They help New Brunswickers get into long-term care. They get people the disability support they qualify for. They protect children and seniors from abuse, they stand behind foster families, and they argue with the system on behalf of people who cannot argue with it themselves.

So: thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, March is National Social Work Month. It is worth taking the time to say what social workers do in New Brunswickers' lives, because most people only find out when they need one.

Over 600 of them work inside the Department of Social Development. That is the department's own count, and it does not take in the ones working in our hospitals, our schools, or First Nations agencies. Those 600-odd help people get into long-term care and onto disability support, protect children and seniors from abuse, back up foster families, and push to get services to people who would otherwise go without.

You will also find social workers in addictions and mental health, with children and youth in care, with seniors, and in women and gender equity work. They offer care, advocacy and support, and they do it with empathy and respect.

Thank you to every one of them. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, and I want to recognize the strength, contributions and resilience of persons with disabilities across this province.

I will admit something. Until I took this file on, I did not know how many separate programs a person has to get through to be helped, and I still could not name them all for you. I am learning. What I do know is that we are committed to building a province in which every person has an equal opportunity to participate fully in our communities, schools, workplaces and public spaces.

This summer we made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit would not detract from provincial disability programs. Federal programs are supposed to complement provincial support, not replace it, and we made that stick.

Accessibility and inclusion are not optional. They are essential to true equity. So let's keep taking the barriers down, one at a time. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Roméo H. LeBlanc is gone, at the age of 102. He was an Acadian veteran of the Second World War. I am the Minister responsible for Military Affairs, and I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country. The war was the short part of it, because for the rest of a very long life he showed up for the veterans' community and made sure that the people who served were remembered by somebody other than their own families. That is unglamorous work. He did it anyway. His life was marked by courage, devotion and a deep sense of duty, and it will be a source of inspiration for this generation and the ones that come after it. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him.

Madam Speaker, I learned with deep sadness of the passing of Roméo H. LeBlanc at the age of 102. He was an Acadian veteran of the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country. I never served myself. I don't know what he carried home from that war, and I am not going to stand here and pretend that I do. What I do know is what he did afterward. He spent his life supporting the veterans' community and preserving the memory of those who served. Courage, devotion, a deep sense of duty — that is the record, and it will be a source of inspiration for generations after ours. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The holidays are on us and I want to talk about local business.

Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. Statistics Canada counts firms with fewer than 100 employees at about 98% of all employers in this country, and that share was already north of 97% a decade ago. Here that means the cafes and restaurants where neighbours gather, the boutiques and artisans who give our downtowns their character, the family-owned shops handed down through two and three generations, and the local producers who keep reminding us that world-class quality is made right here at home. These are not only storefronts. They are employers, they are community supporters, and they are a real part of the economic development of this province.

When we choose to shop locally, especially over the holidays, we are doing more than purchasing a gift. We are investing directly in our communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick — jobs, local supply chains, the foundations under our regional economies. That ripple effect is powerful. It is what lets a small business grow, change and keep serving the community it cares about.

I was at the Premier's open house yesterday. The turnout was strong, stronger than I expected on a Wednesday, and the range of vendors was wide. I spoke to one vendor who started his business at nine years old. Nine. He has been at it longer now than some of the members in this Chamber have been in politics.

So explore the local markets this holiday season, visit the neighbourhood shops, find the artisans, buy New Brunswick-made. Choices big and small make a real difference, and when we support local shopping we support the people who support us all year. A special thank-you to everyone who was out yesterday and spoke to those vendors.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The holidays are nearly here and the main streets are lit up, so I rise to talk about our local businesses.

Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. I mean the cafe on the corner, the two restaurants where neighbours end up on a Friday, the boutiques and artisans who give our downtowns their character, the hardware store a family has run through three generations, and the producer out in the county who keeps proving world-class quality gets made right here at home. Those owners hire people. They sponsor teams, they buy the ad in the rink, and they build up the economy of this province as surely as any big employer does.

When we shop locally at Christmas, we do more than buy a gift. We put money back into our own communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick. It pays wages. It goes to a supplier down the road. It keeps a regional economy standing. That is what lets a small shop grow and keep serving the people around it.

I was at the Premier's open house yesterday. Plenty of people came through, and the vendors ranged from a soap maker to a woodworker to somebody selling smoked salmon. I spoke to one vendor who started his business at nine years old.

Go to the markets this season. Walk into the neighbourhood shops. Find the artisans and buy the New Brunswick-made thing. Choices big and small make a real difference, and when we shop local we support the people who support us all year. A special thank-you to everyone who was out yesterday and spoke to those vendors.

Madam Speaker, we have launched a new provincial website so that more New Brunswickers know what the arts and culture sector is doing here, take part in it and value it. The address is artsculturenb.ca. It puts up painters, potters, fiddlers, furniture makers, and the woman who does the wreaths at the Saturday market, and it landed just in time for the holidays. A New Brunswicker can use it to find a gift, a concert, a play, a studio open house. That money goes to our creative sector and to the people who make our communities better places to live. Artists and artisans can post their own events and their own work on the site themselves. Go to artsculturenb.ca and see what people in this province are making. Shop local this month. Buy from someone who lives here. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, my colleague raised homelessness in Moncton in this House last week, and I want to put a name beside it. Charlie Burrell.

In Little River, Charlie has given his own time and energy to building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who get walked past. He saw his friends on the streets of Moncton. "Friends" is his word, not mine; he uses it every single time, and he does not let you get away with using another one. Instead of turning away, he stepped up. He brings food and clothing, and, more than that, he offers dignity and hope.

He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue, but a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. His efforts pull the community in behind him and get other people involved.

Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Madam Speaker, I want to talk about Charlie Burrell, who shows what one person can do in their community. In Little River, he has put his own time and energy into building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people most of us walk past.

I'm not an expert in housing policy or in addiction, and I won't pretend to be. Charlie doesn't have the credentials either. What he has is that he saw his friends, and that is the word he always uses, sleeping on the streets of Moncton, and he did not turn away. He stepped up. He brings food and clothing, and beyond that he offers dignity and hope.

He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue but a human experience, and that everybody deserves kindness and a chance. Other people see him at it and get involved themselves.

Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford, beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12. I did not know him nearly as well as many of the people who will be in that room this week, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But I know what his family has told me. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. He was a devoted family man and the cornerstone of his family, always putting their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds, and he was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. I am told that warm smile and that infectious laugh could light up a room. His sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. Robert was his family's biggest cheerleader, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. They'll be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into mere ornaments — sparkly, shiny, and completely hollow. First, there was the balanced budget promise, the one we were told would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. The member opposite stood in this House and said the books were "on track". On track. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. It's not even the gift that keeps on giving. It's the gift that keeps on taking. Then, there's the carbon tax adjustor, a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. Instead, it's still there, adding to the prices of everything we buy every day. That's not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. New Brunswickers have been promised a lot of things. This government needs to realize that promises aren't just for the Christmas season. They're for the whole year. It's time they deliver.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict, and peacekeeping. Their courage, sacrifice, and unwavering sense of duty have safeguarded the freedom and values we cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who have returned home changed by their service. As we gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick — the big ones, and the small ones with no parking lot and no sound system, where somebody's brother reads the names off a card — may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.
