Madam Speaker, property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill. That bill comes through Finance and Treasury Board. But they also pay charges through their local tax rates. So the same owner pays twice. First, the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee, printed on the tax bill where anybody can see it; second, the municipal taxes that the municipality turns around and pays to Service New Brunswick for assessment services, which nobody sees at all.

Most people do not know that. They assume the visible charge is the whole cost. It is not.

Let me be clear about one thing. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments. The assessment system itself is important, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts, and I am not standing here to take a run at the people who do that work.

Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. It is charging the cost of assessment fee directly through property tax bills. That is the charge this motion would eliminate. Assessments have risen. Costs have risen. After years of both, the time has come.

People increasingly feel that the government financially benefits from circumstances ordinary citizens cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income requested that their modest home be reassessed at a dramatically higher value. We all know — we all know — that assessments have gone up in recent years, and I said earlier why: COVID-19, people moving to New Brunswick, home prices climbing, and fair market value being a big factor in how the assessment is done. That is why there was such an increase.

Every time those assessments rise, the government revenue from this fee rises as well. That is troubling. It is the perception that government financially benefits from the same assessment increases that cause property owners stress and anxiety.

Madam Speaker, I am not an assessor and I have never worked a day at Service New Brunswick, so if I get a term wrong here, correct me.

Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill, which is through Finance and Treasury Board. But property owners pay charges through their local tax rates as well. So the same property owner is paying both directly and indirectly. First, the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill. Second, the municipal taxes that are used to pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services.

I knock on doors and I can tell you that many New Brunswickers do not know this. They assume the visible charge on the bill is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize that municipalities also pay Service New Brunswick. I did not know it either until a councillor in my riding walked me through her budget line by line at her kitchen table.

Now, I want to be clear about something. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary, and municipalities require accurate assessments. The assessment system itself is important, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and rural districts.

But Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. It is charging the cost of assessment fee directly through property tax bills. That is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate, and after years of rising assessments and rising costs, I would argue the time has come.

People increasingly feel that the government financially benefits from circumstances ordinary citizens cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income requested that their modest home be reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know — we all know — that assessments have gone up in recent years. As I mentioned previously, with COVID-19 and people moving to New Brunswick, home prices have gone up. Fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process, and that is why there was such an increase.

Every time those assessments rise, the government revenue from this fee rises as well. Is that deliberate? I don't know. But it creates the perception that government financially benefits from the same assessment increases that cause property owners stress and anxiety.

Mr. Speaker, labour relations in this province are strained, and that strain sits over every effort we make together to build prosperity in New Brunswick. This government took a legislative approach and that approach is the reason. We should be talking to workers and their representatives directly, telling them the truth, and keeping our word to them. Workers will trust a government that does those things, and a government that has their trust can weigh what everybody at the table needs.

Mr. Speaker, in December 2019, this Legislature was embroiled in a contentious debate over the essential service legislation, which was specifically focused on the wages of nursing home workers. That bill, Bill 17, imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on the wages of those workers. It sparked an intense reaction. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions came out against it. They said it would damage their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage, and they said it loudly. You could hear how deep the discontent ran.

The law passed. Union leaders decried it as an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced. She said they would keep fighting for better working conditions and keep protecting the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society.

Bill 17 showed how the government and the labour unions in New Brunswick pull against each other on labour rights and on collective bargaining. It showed how hard it is to weigh what a worker needs against what a taxpayer pays and what a finance minister has to answer for.

When we look back at December 2019 and at the passage of Bill 17, we can't forget that there are members sitting in this government now who opposed that bill. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with the labour movement as long as they could. That has changed today.

We are building a system where mental health care and addiction care work hand in hand. Honestly, I am not a clinician and I have never worked in addictions treatment, so I am relying here on the people who do. What they tell me is that these challenges are usually connected in the same person and have to be addressed together.

So we are integrating the services, and the province is creating a seamless continuum of care that spans prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction. That gets people the right supports at every stage of their journey. For children and youth, it means early community-based interventions that can prevent substance use from escalating and reduce long-term harms. For someone already living with addiction, it means timely access to a full range of treatment options: detox services, live-in programs, outpatient counselling, and long-term recovery supports.

Our investments reflect this. The Moncton Addictions and Mental Health Court will offer those facing mental health and addiction challenges an opportunity to access treatment and community supports when they come into contact with the justice system. It gives someone facing criminal charges an alternative pathway to traditional sentencing, connecting them to treatment and recovery supports while easing pressures on the justice system and improving long-term outcomes for participants.

This week we took the first step to expand treatment capacity, and we announced a new 50-bed addiction treatment facility. Is 50 enough? I don't know. I doubt it. We are actively exploring further opportunities to increase the number of treatment beds across New Brunswick.

Well, beds are no good without staff. That is why there are 10 newly established trainer positions dedicated to building the skills, expertise, and resilience of the addictions and mental health workforce. Together, these efforts will strengthen service delivery, create consistency across the province, and help ensure people living with substance use challenges receive the right care at the right time and in the right setting.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the Battle of Vimy Ridge. It was fought on April 9, 1917. It is one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has worked at raising awareness of that battle and educating Canadians about it, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary in 2027, which I hope every school in my riding takes part in, because a date on a page does not mean much to a 14-year-old unless somebody in the room makes it mean something. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9. Wear the pin. The Vimy Pin is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge, and it stands for their unity and their sacrifice. That is what we are honouring. Their courage. The legacy they left behind, which helped define this nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. I am no military historian, and I could not tell you much about how the ridge was taken. But I know what the date means. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle, and this year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the battle in 2027. So as we approach Vimy Week, from April 2 to 9, I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, and I had to be told this last year — one colour for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge, standing for their unity and their sacrifice. By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice, and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, October 24 was Laura Anderson's 105th birthday, and Newtown turned out for it. She is still in her own house and still independent. She had her driver's licence until this past month and used it, mostly for short runs along Route 890. Laura and Thomas were pioneers in agriculture and in tourism in this province. Founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick. They kept the farming heritage from being thrown out with the machinery. In 1967 they opened New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience, and people came from across the province and from around the world to sleep on a working farm. The humour is still there. So are the stories. I congratulate her on 105 years and I thank her for what she has given this province. She takes her tea black and her opinions plain.

Madam Speaker, last September we started a universal breakfast program in every school in New Brunswick. It has been close to a year, and we can see what it does. Students eat in the morning now: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, cheese, and, in one school I was in, a pan of leftover baked beans. FeedNB works with the schools, and much of the food comes off farms and out of businesses here at home. Parents tell us the program saves them time and money, and it takes some of the noise out of the house at seven in the morning. That counts for more when groceries cost what they cost now. A child who has eaten can sit down and learn something. That is what we paid for. Every child should be able to start the day fed, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, last September our government put a universal breakfast program into every school in New Brunswick. I have not been in all of them — I have been in maybe a dozen — but in the ones I have seen, it is working. Milk, eggs, bagels, apples, cheese. FeedNB gets it there, and a good deal of it comes off farms and out of businesses here at home. I don't have the uptake numbers in front of me today, and I should. What I do hear from parents is that it saves them money and saves them the argument at half past seven, and with grocery prices where they are, that is not nothing. A kid who has eaten can concentrate. That is the investment. Every child deserves to start the day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, the member opposite asked yesterday what exactly is "historic" about this capital budget. I will answer that. It is $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, and the largest capital budget ever tabled in this province. When we resolve into the Committee of Supply on the capital estimates, the member can go line by line with the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, because most of this money is his: roads, bridges, ferries, and the other essential infrastructure. Health care is next, for modernizing medical equipment and renovating hospitals. Education gets new schools in Shediac and in Moncton, and upgrades to several institutions elsewhere in the province. My colleague has been raising that Shediac school since before I got here. The word the member opposite should be quarrelling with is not "historic." It is "backlog." Years of underinvestment built it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Deputy Speaker, Premier Higgs took nursing home workers to court. He told them to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages. Those are the people who lift our parents out of bed, who feed them, who sit with them at the end. A premier who says that to them has not failed at negotiating. He has told them what he thinks they are worth.

The school strike lasted 16 days. It ended when this government signed emergency orders and ordered the workers back into the buildings. A government cannot say it believes in bargaining and in the right to strike and then do that.

This government watered down binding arbitration. It brought in scab-friendly legislation. Now it brings us this pension bill. Custodians, bus drivers, educational assistants, laundry staff, and the woman who does the payroll for all of them — every one of them loses a little more ground each time.

Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions and their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate this government proposed in its early years. Zero percent. In a global pandemic, our frontline workers were heroes, and this government offered them zero. They earned more than a round of applause from this Chamber. They earned money. The union leaders said it better than I will: these heroes deserved more than zeroes.

When a government decides these things, somebody's mortgage moves. Somebody's daughter takes the job in Fort McMurray. We are here to question that, and I question it. A fair society lets a worker bargain across the table as an equal, and this one has spent five years making sure she cannot.

Madam Speaker, the member opposite used the word "withdrawal" three times this morning. That is not the word. This approach refocuses public resources on their core mission and leaves the routine care to private veterinarians, who are already doing most of it. The goal is a more modern and sustainable model, in line with Canadian best practices, so that veterinary services in this province still work five and ten years from now.

The member also said, and I wrote it down, that a farm is a farm. It is not. The needs of an operation in Kings County and the needs of one up the Restigouche are different, and the model has to meet both.

I will grant my colleague this much: the implementation is causing concern, and the government recognizes it. In the remote regions the concerns are the cost of the service and the quality of it, and in several of those regions access was already a considerable challenge before any of this. That is why a support program for private sector veterinarians is being developed, to offset costs such as travel, so that producers in every region continue to get the services they need.

Those answers have not cleared up all the worries. I would not claim they have.

On laboratories: the member for Victoria-La Vallée asked last Thursday whether the labs close. They do not. The existing laboratories remain fully operational through the transition — early detection of emerging diseases, prevention of health crises, food safety — so that no farmer and no veterinarian is disrupted.

When this goes to the Standing Committee on Economic Policy, bring the objections. We are still open to hearing your opinions, your ideas, and your worries, and this only works if people participate.

Madam Speaker, I am not a veterinarian, and I did not grow up on a farm. I have had to learn this file from the people who live it. Here is what the change does: it refocuses public resources on their core mission and leaves the routine care to private veterinarians. We are not withdrawing. We are moving to a more modern and sustainable model, in line with Canadian best practices, so the service is there for farms now and in the future.

The government recognizes that the implementation is causing concerns. In the remote regions, producers are asking what the service will cost and whether the quality will hold, and in several of those regions access was already a considerable challenge. So a support program for private sector veterinarians is being developed to offset some of their costs, travel in particular. I don't have the final figure for that program and I am not going to invent one at this microphone.

Have our answers cleared up all the worries? No. I have sat in enough kitchens now to know they have not.

Laboratory services are a key part of the transition — early detection of emerging diseases, prevention of health crises, food safety. Through the transition the existing laboratories stay fully operational, so no farmer and no veterinarian loses working time to this.

I would rather build the consensus now than defend the thing later. We are still open to your opinions, your ideas, and your worries. It is a big transformation, and whether it works will depend on whether producers and veterinarians choose to come along.

Mr. Speaker, the minister said in this House on Tuesday that public transportation is "already covered off" between his department and the municipalities. I wrote the words down. It is not covered off. The From Surfaces to Services report was tabled in 2017, it said this province needed one coordinated approach to public transportation, and since then nothing meaningful has been done with it. The member opposite is welcome to stand up and name the department that wrote the strategy. No one did.

Give one minister the file and you have somebody who leads it, pays for it, and stands here to answer for how the pieces fit together across New Brunswick.

BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation;

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the government to allocate the necessary resources and funding to support the New Brunswick Transportation Authority to create and implement a public transportation strategy.

(Debate adjourned.)

Mr. Speaker, the From Surfaces to Services report was tabled in 2017. It said the province needed one coordinated approach to public transportation. Nothing meaningful has been done with it since, and in the meantime the same people — students, seniors, the fellow working the back shift who lost his licence — are told to find their own way to wherever it is they have to be, in a province where the cost of keeping a car on the road has gotten out of hand. Eight years. Nothing.

Put a minister in charge of it and somebody has to lead it, fund it, and answer here when it fails. That's the whole idea.

BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation;

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Legislative Assembly urge the government to allocate the necessary resources and funding to support the New Brunswick Transportation Authority to create and implement a public transportation strategy.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise to propose a resolution calling on the government to take action to protect the health of New Brunswickers after COVID-19.

Now, I am not a public health physician. I have never run an outbreak response, and there are members here who follow the epidemiology far better than I do. But I sat through the same briefings everyone else did, and over the break I finally read the Public Health Act, which I probably should have done years ago.

Here is what I take from it. The Act is the cornerstone of how this province answers a pandemic and it is out of date. RSV belongs in it. There should be a straightforward mechanism for Public Health to add an illness to the list it tracks, and as far as I can find, there isn't one. If I have that wrong, I would like the minister to tell me so.

Being prepared is not free. It is infrastructure and it is people. Well, mostly it is people. Two winters ago the clinic in my riding was running with staff pulled off other duties, and one of them told me she had not had a day off in five weeks.

So we need the public education piece too, running early, in plain language, before anybody is frightened.

And we know who gets hurt worst: seniors, people with underlying conditions, and people in communities that were already short of care. I don't know how you write that into a statute properly. I do know that a plan written for the average New Brunswicker will not find them, because it didn't last time.

I ask members to support the resolution calling on the government to amend the Public Health Act and to put real strategies behind it. We were not ready. I include myself in that.

Mr. Speaker, this is a government that took nursing home workers to court. That is where we ended up — the Premier in a courtroom against the people who bathe and feed our parents, and then telling them, when they gathered outside, to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages.

The offer on the table was 10.5 cents an hour. Ten and a half cents. On a 37.5-hour week that is $3.94, and something like $205 over a year, in a year when Statistics Canada had grocery prices running 10% to 11% above the year before. Those two numbers do not sit beside each other honestly.

Then came binding arbitration with conditions attached, which is not arbitration. The conditions were the point. Attaching them was a way to keep the workers' actual demands off the table before anybody sat down at it.

His words to the protesters were, "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." That is dismissive, and it ignores what these workers are up against here. Instead of dealing with what was in front of him, the Premier deflected.

And he told us that fair wages would not fix the staffing shortage in our nursing homes. A fair wage is a matter of justice for the worker, yes. It is also the recruitment and retention tool the province has been refusing to pick up.

He never treated it as urgent. He never sat down with them in any meaningful way. His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick, and we are going to keep reminding him of it.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from the other side used the phrase "a fair process" a few minutes ago, and I would like to test it against the record.

This government took nursing home workers to court. The Premier proposed binding arbitration with conditions attached — his side calls that "arbitration," and I say a conditional arbitration is not arbitration at all, because the conditions decide the outcome before anyone sits down. The insistence on it was a way around the legitimate concerns those workers brought forward.

He would not go above 10.5 cents an hour. Ten and a half cents, for the people who feed and bathe our parents.

And then, to protesters outside, the words were these: "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." I have heard members opposite say that was taken out of context. Give me the context. He said it to their faces, and it showed exactly how much he understood about what those workers were carrying.

The Premier also asserted in this House that fair wages will not address the staffing shortage in New Brunswick nursing homes. A fair wage is justice for the worker. It is also the recruitment and retention measure this province has refused to use.

Instead of dialogue, we got confrontation and division. His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick, and we will remind him of that over and over again.

Mr. Speaker, this government took nursing home workers to court. I want to say that again, because I think people at home stopped believing it when they heard it the first time. This government took nursing home workers to court, and the Premier told them to go to Alberta if they wanted better wages.

His offer was 10.5 cents an hour. Ten and a half cents an hour. That is what the people who bathe and feed our parents were worth to him at the table.

Then came binding arbitration with conditions. Conditions. Attach conditions and you have not agreed to arbitration, you have written the answer in advance, and that is a way of never dealing with what those workers came to say.

The words to the protesters were, "if you want that kind of wage, then Alberta's where to get it." I repeat — "Alberta's where to get it." That was said out loud, in this province, to New Brunswickers doing that work.

And then he told us fair wages will not fix the staffing shortage in our nursing homes. A fair wage is justice for the worker, and it is also how you keep one. He never treated any of it as urgent.

His responsibility is to the people of New Brunswick. Not to Alberta. To the people of New Brunswick.

Madam Speaker, a new family health team was announced in Bathurst yesterday. Clinics like it keep opening around the province, and each one puts more primary care within reach of the people living around it.

For the Chaleur region it is a plain improvement. More professionals under one roof. Intake that bends a bit. Referrals that go where they are supposed to go instead of back to the family.

Nursing Home Without Walls was in the room. So was the mayor, and so was Sylvie, who has been running the Wednesday foot care clinic out of a church basement for eleven years and who told me she would take the parking lot over the ribbon.

The collaborative model is slowly changing how care gets delivered here. Promise made, promise kept, Madam Speaker.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act, which already sets out how we review patient safety incidents and learn from them. The government says the amendments will improve those reviews, strengthen collaboration, make things more consistent and improve transparency for patients and families. I am not going to argue against any of that. But a bill gets judged on what it does, not on what it hoped to do.

Now, I am not a clinician. I have never sat on a quality review committee and I would not pretend to know how one runs from the inside. What I can read is the bill, and what I keep looking for in it is the problem. The existing Act already provides the framework. So what failed? At the briefing those questions were asked and they were fair ones. The government has not shown us data on a systemic failure under the current law. Without that we are legislating in search of a problem.

The largest change is the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper, fine. Who opposes expert advice?

But slow down. Professionals here already answer to Horizon, to Vitalité, to their colleges, to accreditation bodies, to internal quality review committees, to the patient advocate. I asked a nurse in Sussex in February how many separate incident forms she fills out and she started counting on her fingers and gave up at four. That is the answer I keep getting.

So I don't know whether this committee improves an outcome or adds a layer. I would like to be convinced. If it becomes one more place to file a report and nothing measurable changes, we will have added weight to a system that is already carrying too much of it, and the people who feel that weight are not in this Chamber.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize Nursing Home Without Walls. The program makes a real difference for seniors in our communities. Today it is partnered with Horizon Health Network at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., giving seniors hands-on help to set up access to MyHealthNB, the secure online portal that lets a person view their own blood work and their own imaging results instead of waiting on a phone call or a letter in the mail. Staff will walk them through it. All you need is a Medicare card and an email address. That is it. Horizon staff verify who you are and give you the access code right there. No appointment. No registration. A senior who can see her own blood work is a senior who stays connected to her own health and stays independent longer. That is the point of it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Nursing Home Without Walls is at it again. Today the program and Horizon Health Network are set up in the main lobby of the Miramichi Regional Hospital, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., getting seniors onto MyHealthNB, where you can view your own blood work and your own imaging results. Past the gift shop, first tables on the left. Bring a Medicare card and an email address, and that is all that is required to create an account. Horizon staff verify identity and give out the access code on the spot. No appointment. No registration. This is another barrier coming down, and it is the one that stops most people — not the technology, the sign-up. Seniors stay connected to their own health information, and they stay healthy and independent. Bring the card. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk have written a cookbook. It is called Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. I have a copy on the counter at home. This is not just a cookbook, Mr. Speaker. The recipes come with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, the people of Mi'gma'gi. The book also takes on gastrocolonialism — how colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes — and it does that plainly, dish by dish. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a cook, and I am not the member anyone should be asking about recipes. I can tell you about a book. Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck, of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, have published Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It is not just a cookbook. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, the people of Mi'gma'gi. I had not heard the word gastrocolonialism before I read it. It is what colonial policies did to traditional Indigenous recipes, and these two authors take it on directly rather than around the edges. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Mr. Speaker, two authors from L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, have done something remarkable. Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck have published Mitji — Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. This is not just a cookbook. The recipes are enriched with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, the people of Mi'gma'gi. Through their work, the authors have addressed gastrocolonialism — how colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions. And I would tell members to go and get the book. Mine already has two pages stuck together.

Madam Speaker, the aim of this bill is to make things easier, not to approve them. It removes barriers. It provides clarity. It puts New Brunswick in a position to move forward when the time comes. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments, including the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, ensuring financial accountability and risk mitigation. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. I am going to say that one more time, because I have been asked about it twice today: it will be reviewed before any authorization. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future — a bold and necessary investment. This bill ensures that we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. I urge all members of the House to support the bill and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I have heard the word "approve" from across the floor a few times this afternoon, and that is the word I want to quarrel with. The bill's aim is to make things easier, not approve them. It is about removing barriers, providing clarity, and ensuring that New Brunswick is prepared to move forward when the time comes. My colleague opposite asked who was at the table. The proposal was drafted in consultation with several departments, including the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, and that is where financial accountability and risk mitigation sit. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill makes sure we meet its challenges with the flexibility and the clarity that will be required. I urge all members of the House to support it and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Employees need 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave. That lines up with the leave provisions in other provinces. They have to tell their employer as soon as possible that they need it, and the employer may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. That is not a hurdle. It keeps the leave sound, and it gives the employer something to plan around, which matters a great deal to a small operator who has to cover a shift on short notice for the better part of half a year. Madam Speaker, this amendment is a step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at the time they are most vulnerable, and it does that without ignoring what workplaces across this province actually look like. It also keeps New Brunswick a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. There is a clear gap in our current legislation. This closes it. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, the member opposite asked earlier what stops this from being abused, so let me answer with the actual text. An employee must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. The employee is required to inform the employer "as soon as possible" of the need for leave — those are the words in the amendment, and they are not "whenever it suits the employee", as I heard put a few minutes ago. The employer may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. Those elements support the integrity of the leave and give employers reasonable assurance and predictability. Madam Speaker, this amendment is an important step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at a time when they are most vulnerable while keeping a balance that considers the realities of workplaces across the province, and it supports the objective of New Brunswick remaining a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. This closes a clear gap in the Employment Standards Act. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I thank the Minister of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour for his statement on the InnovateNB Awards, and I join him in recognizing this year's recipients. They are pushing boundaries and driving progress in this province, and that deserves the House's notice. The minister used the phrase "growing confidence" in New Brunswick's business climate. I wrote it down. Growing where, and for whom? I would put it to him that confidence is not shared equally across all sectors and communities, and I've heard the member for Campbellton-Dalhousie say much the same thing in this Chamber twice this fall. Innovation does not exist in a vacuum. It requires a supportive ecosystem, and the barriers many innovators face here have not moved. Our rural areas still struggle to access the resources and the support that urban centres enjoy. The benefits have to reach every corner of the province and not just those with established networks. The recipients are inspiring, but I want to ask the minister what we are doing to cultivate the next generation. Investments in education, mentorship programs, and accessible funds are essential if our youth are going to lead the charge. And while we celebrate, we still need continued investment in research and development, particularly in clean technology and sustainable practices, the sectors that align with the economic goals this government has set out. When the estimates for the department come before the Committee of Supply, I intend to ask about exactly that. Government, industry, and communities working together is the only way an inclusive environment gets built. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. I'll say that again: clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at approved farmers' markets, something that small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for. The ability of a microbrewery or craft distillery to connect directly with customers at a local market, whether it's the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. It recognizes the growth of a sector that has truly taken off here in New Brunswick. That said, modernization should never come without scrutiny. This bill sets production caps for breweries and distilleries: 500 000 L for brewers, and 75 000 L for distillers. That's when they are operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation. Now, those sound like fair limits, but we need to ask: Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier? We've seen this before — we've seen this before — where well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays. Craft producers in St. Croix and elsewhere in New Brunswick, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. That is what they told me, and I am repeating it word for word. This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our economic development strategy has one priority: build a stronger, more competitive New Brunswick that gives people here somewhere to go. New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. When a company grows, reaches a new market, and puts money back into its own operation, it hires people, it holds a community together, and it pays into the tax base that funds the services families use every single day. The strategy builds on what we already have. It aims at productivity. It backs the firms that are trying something new, and it helps New Brunswick companies compete in a global economy that will not sit still for them. We are also going after investment and building up the sectors where we can actually win — defence and mining chief among them — and we want that growth to last. Departments will work off the same list of priorities and the same measurable outcomes, and I will be answerable for them. The government cannot do this alone. It takes industry, the universities and colleges, communities, and frankly every member sitting in this House. The people we have shown it to so far like what they see, and what they keep coming back to is that it is clear, it is disciplined, and it says what it will deliver. New Brunswick has what the world wants. We are competing to win, and we are setting the conditions for businesses to grow, for communities to thrive, and for opportunity to spread out past the two or three places that usually get it. A growing economy pays for better services. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built. The Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, came to the region in February and made the announcement themselves. It was blowing sideways that morning, as it does. I thank them both. That announcement marks a turning point for our communities. The bridge will simplify travel, strengthen our connections with the rest of the province, and bring new economic opportunities to our people. On behalf of my constituents, I want to express our gratitude to everyone who played a role in making this important project happen. Wela'lin. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I am pleased to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association to the gallery today. Several of their Board of Directors are with them. A few drove in this morning — Saint John, Bathurst, one from farther than that, in the rain. Their work is essential to supporting New Brunswickers' mental health and well-being, and the association's continued collaboration with the Department of Health is helping to strengthen our system of care. I will have more to say on that a little later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, it was with deep sadness that I learned of the passing, at the age of 102, of Roméo H. LeBlanc, an Acadian veteran of the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his service to this country. He did more than serve. For decades afterward he looked after other veterans, and he made sure the ones who did not come back were still spoken of by name. He was courageous and he was dutiful, and people who come across his story will take something from it. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my condolences to his family, his loved ones, and the veterans' community. We will remember him. His family tells me he kept his medals in the top drawer of the dresser, in a cigar box. Not on a wall. In a drawer.

Madam Speaker, Roméo H. LeBlanc has died at the age of 102. He was an Acadian veteran of the Second World War, and as Minister responsible for Military Affairs I want to pay tribute to him. I should say that I met him once, and briefly, so most of what I know about him I know secondhand. I am not going to stand here and tell members I understand what he saw overseas. I don't. What I can speak to is the part after. He spent the rest of his life with the veterans' community, and he worked to keep the memory of those who served from slipping away. He was courageous and he was dutiful. Younger people will find something in that. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my condolences to his family, to his loved ones, and to the veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, artsculturenb.ca launched this week. It is a provincial site and it is live in time for the holiday season. It showcases artists, artisans, and cultural experiences here in New Brunswick, and it will help people find a local gift, an event, or a performance to get to over the next few weeks. Anyone working in arts and culture can upload their own events and their own creations to it. Frye Jam is on there. So is the Sussex quilt show, which I only know about because my sister-in-law entered. The point is awareness — people knowing what is being made around them, and thinking better of it. Visit artsculturenb.ca. Shop local this season, and support the artists who make this province extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell shows what one person can do. In Little River he has spent his own time and his own energy building a facility and small homes for people who have nowhere to live — people most of us walk past. He saw his friends, and he calls them his friends every single time, homeless on the streets of Moncton, and instead of turning away he did something. He brings them food and clothing. More than that, he treats them like people. He keeps saying that homelessness is not an issue, it is something happening to somebody, and that everyone is owed some kindness and a chance. Others have got involved because he asked them to. Thank you, Charlie. The last time I was out there, he was arguing with a fellow about the price of plywood and losing. The homes have doors that lock. That is the part he wanted me to mention.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell is an example of what one person can do in their community. In Little River, he has put his time and his own energy into building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who get overlooked and forgotten. He saw his friends, and that is the word he always uses, homeless on the streets of Moncton, and he stepped up instead of turning away. He gives out food and clothing, and, more than that, he gives people dignity and some hope.

I will be honest with members. I am not an expert on housing policy or on addiction, and I do not know whether what Charlie is doing in Little River can be done anywhere else at any scale. I have asked. I have not got a good answer yet. What I do know is that in February there was a man sleeping in a car behind the Irving, and by March that man had a room with a door on it. Charlie has pulled other people in behind him, and more of them turn up every month.

He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue, it is a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. Change starts with one person choosing to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Madam Speaker, the Act as written says the executive committee has no quorum unless the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy is present. That person, or their delegate, is a non-voting member. The idea was economic alignment across government. What it has produced is scheduling trouble and delayed decisions whenever that deputy head cannot be there.

The amendment before the House is straightforward. Quorum becomes a simple majority of voting members present.

Members are entitled to ask what this costs us. How many meetings has the current rule actually lost us in the past two years? Three? A dozen? Is that even the thing holding this committee back? I do not have those numbers in front of me today.

What I can tell members is what the amendment does not do. It does not alter the composition of the executive committee. It does not alter the participation of the deputy head whose mandate has a direct impact on the economy. That individual remains a valued contributor to the committee's work.

We made the same change for the board of directors in 2021, when the "quorum" definition in this Act was simplified for the board. This brings the two into line.

The committee will be able to meet and conduct its business without unnecessary disruption. In a fast-paced economic environment, the ability to act swiftly and effectively matters. Opportunities New Brunswick will be better positioned to deliver programs, to respond to emerging opportunities, and to keep supporting the businesses that drive our province's growth.

It is an administrative change. It will matter to the operation of that committee. I encourage all members to support it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford — beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12. He left behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. He was a devoted family man. He was the cornerstone of his family, and he put their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds. If you needed a hand, or you needed somebody to sit and listen, Robert was there. His warm smile and that infectious laugh could light up a room, and his sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. He was his family's biggest cheerleader, proudly supporting whatever they took on and celebrating every success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Pop pop. That is what the grandchildren called him.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford, beloved husband, father, pop pop, uncle, great-uncle, and friend. Robert passed away on Wednesday, November 12, leaving behind a legacy of love, laughter, and adventure. He was a devoted family man. He was the cornerstone of his family — the cornerstone — always putting their needs before his own. I want to say that again, because his family said it to me twice: he put their needs before his own. His love and support knew no bounds, and he was always there to lend a helping hand or offer a listening ear. Robert's warm smile and infectious laugh could light up a room, and his sense of humour could turn even the toughest day into a memorable moment. He was his family's biggest cheerleader, proudly supporting their endeavours and celebrating their success. Whether he was cheering on his favourite team or teaching a lesson, his passion for sports was only matched by his love for his family. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and friends. Thank you.

Too often, the subsidies and the incentives go to large corporations. Not to the small and medium-sized businesses that create most of the local jobs in our communities. That is backwards. Direct that investment to smaller businesses instead and the wealth generated by economic activity stays in New Brunswick communities, in the towns where it was earned in the first place. One idea that has been suggested is stronger support for community economic development corporations, which allow residents to invest directly in businesses by purchasing community investment shares. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have done it. Hundreds of enterprises have been launched under those models, including renewable energy projects and community-based ventures. It works. With provincial support and promotion, it could work here too. Citizens raised energy as well. The message was not complicated. Stop leaning on large, high-risk megaprojects. There is growing support for a diversified approach focused on efficiency and renewables: an energy investment fund to help new technologies reach commercialization, a modest levy on electrical bills dedicated to efficiency and renewable projects, and a Property Assessed Clean Energy program to fund solar installations, battery storage and efficiency upgrades. Household costs would come down. Skilled jobs would go up. And the long-term electrical demand challenge NB Power is facing gets a little easier, which is not a sentence I get to say often in this Chamber. Then there is procurement. Every year the provincial government spends tens of millions of dollars on goods and services. Much of that money leaves. It goes to large corporations, or to suppliers outside this province, and it does not come back. Send even a small portion of it to local businesses, cooperatives and social enterprises and you have created something real. Hospitals, universities, schools and correctional facilities buy much the same things year after year. Redirect a small share of those contracts and it ripples.

Madam Speaker, on November 11 we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict and peacekeeping. Their courage, their sacrifice and their unwavering sense of duty safeguarded the freedom and the values we cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who returned home changed by their service. Next Tuesday I will be at the cenotaph in Oromocto. The parade forms up at the Legion, the way it has for as long as anyone there can tell me, and it will be cold. Poppies will be left on the stone afterward and somebody will collect them. As people gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick, may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict and peacekeeping. Their courage, their sacrifice and their unwavering sense of duty safeguarded the freedom and the values we cherish today. I have never served. I don't know what that is, and I am not going to stand here and pretend I do. So I will say the part I do understand. We pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who returned home changed by their service. My uncle came back and did not talk about it for forty years, and then one afternoon at the kitchen table he did, for about ten minutes. As we gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick, may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget.

Madam Speaker, on October 24 our community marked the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson of Newtown. Laura is strong, she is sharp, and she still lives on her own in her own house. Until just this past month she kept her driver's licence and took short drives out the rural roads she has driven for most of her life. She knows where every washout is on them. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were pioneers in farming and in tourism in this province. The two of them helped found the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick, and that museum still holds equipment they saved from the scrap pile. In 1967 they opened the first farm vacation in New Brunswick. Families came out from Saint John, from Quebec, from the United States, from England, and one summer from Australia. Laura still tells the stories, and she still gets the timing right. We congratulate her on 105 years and we thank her for what she and Thomas built.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in every New Brunswick school. Close to a year later, the results are showing up. Every morning, right across the province, students are starting the day on milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. FeedNB gets it there. Much of it is grown or made here, on our own farms and in our own businesses; the yogurt in one of my schools comes out of Sussex. For a lot of families, with prices where they are, this program is making a real difference. It saves parents time and money, and it takes the fight out of the morning routine. Students get to class ready to learn, able to concentrate, and willing to take part. This is a concrete investment in the success of our young people. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. It works. Close to a year later we are already seeing concrete results, with students in every corner of the province starting the day on a nutritious meal of milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools can offer healthy food that is often grown right here, on our own farms and in our own businesses. For many families, with the cost of living rising the way it has, this program makes a real difference. It saves them money. It saves them time. The morning is less of a fight. And students arrive in class prepared to learn, able to concentrate, and willing to take part in the lesson instead of watching the clock until lunch. That matters. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget. It is $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, and it is the largest capital budget this province has ever tabled. The Department of Transportation and Infrastructure takes most of it. That department will pave roads, replace bridges, keep the ferries running, and fix the wharf ramps nobody talks about until one of them fails. Our hospitals will see significant money as well, to replace medical equipment and to renovate the buildings themselves. We are building a new school in Shediac and a new school in Moncton, and we are upgrading institutions elsewhere in the province. Crews left much of this work sitting for years because previous budgets did not pay for it, and that backlog is what we are now paying down. Parents drive their children over these bridges every morning. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget, a historic budget of $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year and the largest capital budget ever tabled in our province. The member opposite called it, yesterday, "an election-year road budget." Those were his words, and I would ask him to look at where the money actually goes. Most of the investment is allocated to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, to improve our roads, bridges, ferries, and other essential infrastructure. The health care sector will also see significant investment, to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate our hospitals. In education, the capital budget includes building new schools in Shediac and Moncton and upgrading several institutions elsewhere in the province. These investments are essential to deal with the backlog caused by years of underinvestment. When this House resolves itself into the Committee of Supply to open the capital estimates, I invite the member to test every line of it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Moreover, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. This government took them to court. Took them to court. Then it suggested they relocate to Alberta for better wages, and I will say that again, because members opposite sigh every time I do: relocate to Alberta for better wages. That was not only a failure in negotiation but also a betrayal of the individuals who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. It reflected a lack of empathy and a failure to prioritize the well-being of those on the front lines. Then there was the 16-day school strike and the subsequent use of emergency orders to force workers back to work. Sixteen days. Those orders raised questions about the government's commitment to meaningful dialogue and about the right to strike, and the use of such measures undermined the very principles of a fair and balanced negotiation process. Watering down binding arbitration. Scab-friendly legislation. This pension bill. That is a pattern of behaviour that erodes the foundation of workers' rights, and these actions do not align with the principles of a just and equitable society that respects the contributions of its workforce. The decisions made by government impact the livelihoods of countless individuals and the overall health of our communities. It is our duty to scrutinize and question these policies that undermine the values we hold dear, values of fairness and respect and the right of workers to negotiate on an equal footing. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate proposed by the Higgs government, the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. Zero percent. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes, and their unwavering commitment and sacrifices demanded not only acknowledgement but also tangible support. The union leaders said it better than I can: these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements.

Moreover, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. I am not a labour lawyer, and I have not read every page of those court filings. I haven't. But I know this government took nursing home workers to court, and I know it suggested they relocate to Alberta for better wages. Well, that was a failure in negotiation, and it was a betrayal of the individuals who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. I met one of them in October; she works two jobs and drives 40 minutes to each of them. There is an argument that a government has to hold a line on wages, and I understand it. But then came the 16-day school strike and the emergency orders used to force workers back to work, and I don't know how anyone squares an emergency order with a commitment to meaningful dialogue or with the right to strike. The use of such measures undermined the very principles of a fair and balanced negotiation process. So look at the sequence: binding arbitration watered down, scab-friendly legislation introduced, and this pension bill now in front of us. I think that is a pattern of behaviour, and it erodes the foundation of workers' rights. These actions do not align with the principles of a just and equitable society that respects the contributions of its workforce. The decisions we make in this building impact the livelihoods of countless individuals and the overall health of our communities, and it is our duty to scrutinize and question policies that undermine the values we hold dear, values of fairness and respect and the right of workers to negotiate on an equal footing. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate proposed by the Higgs government, the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. Their commitment and their sacrifices demanded tangible support, not just acknowledgement. Let me be straight with the House. I am not a veterinarian, and I have never had to call one out at two in the morning for a calving gone wrong. So I have done a lot of listening on this file. This approach allows public resources to be refocused on their core mission while leveraging the expertise of the private sector for the delivery of routine care. We are not withdrawing. The goal is a more modern and sustainable model, aligned with Canadian best practices, so that veterinary services stay robust and are adapted to current and future challenges. The modernization will enable New Brunswick to build a model that can meet the specific needs of farms while guaranteeing high-quality services. I will admit that we did not get ahead of the concerns the implementation has caused. For remote regions there are real challenges concerning the quality and the cost of services, and in several of those regions access was already a considerable challenge before any of this began. A producer in Kent County told me last month that he waited eleven hours. That is why a support program for private sector veterinarians is being developed. One of its objectives is to help offset certain costs, like travel expenses, so that producers from all regions can continue to get the services they need. The responses that have been provided do not mean all the worries have been cleared up. I don't think they have. But they underscore our commitment to finding concrete solutions tailored to each situation. Laboratory services are a key part of the transition. They do the early detection of emerging diseases, they prevent health crises, and they underpin food safety, and the existing laboratories will remain fully operational throughout, so that no farmer's or veterinarian's work is disrupted. We still need consensus around what we are proposing, and its success will depend in large part on cooperation and on people choosing to take part with an open mind. I am still open to hearing your opinions, your ideas, and your worries. I have already changed my mind on one part of this.

This approach lets the province put its own money and its own people back on the work only the province can do, and lets private practices handle the routine calls, because that is where the expertise already sits. We are not walking away. We want a model that is more modern, that lasts, and that lines up with how the rest of Canada does this, so that a farmer can still get a vet who knows what is coming at that farm now and in ten years. New Brunswick can build that model around what farms actually need, and the quality of the work does not have to drop to do it. We know the change is worrying people. In remote regions, producers are asking what a call will cost and who will answer it, and in several of those regions they were already waiting too long before we touched anything. So we are building a support program for private sector veterinarians. It will offset costs such as travel, so a producer in Restigouche can get the same visit as a producer twenty minutes from Sussex. What we have said so far has not settled every worry. It does show that we mean to fix these things case by case. The labs matter here. Our labs catch an emerging disease early, they stop an outbreak before it moves, and they keep the food supply safe, and every existing lab stays open through the whole transition so that no farmer and no veterinarian loses a day's work waiting on a result. We still have to agree on this, and I want to hear your opinions, your ideas, and your worries. This is a big change, and it will only work if the people it lands on decide to take part.

Bill 40 proposes significant amendments to the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already sets up a framework for reviewing and learning from patient safety incidents. According to the government, the amendments aim to improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, enhance consistency, and improve transparency for patients and families. Those are worthy objectives. No reasonable person opposes a system that learns better.

But legislation is judged by its consequences, not its intentions, and as we examine Bill 40 closely, several questions arise. Before we create new structures or grant new powers: what specific problem is this bill trying to address? The existing Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews, so what has failed? Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? Are health authorities ignoring recommendations? These concerns were raised during the briefing, and rightfully so. Legislative changes should follow demonstrated gaps. The government has not presented clear data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we risk legislating in search of a problem rather than solving one.

One of the most significant changes is the creation of a New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, to be established and maintained by the minister. On paper this sounds reasonable. Who could oppose expert advice on patient safety?

Here is where prudence requires us to slow down. Health care professionals in this province already operate within multiple oversight structures: Horizon, Vitalite, the colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees, patient advocacy offices. I was at the Chalmers in February. The staff there did not ask me for another committee. They are already telling us they spend increasing amounts of time filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this becomes another reporting layer without measurable improvement, we will have unintentionally worsened the very system we set out to protect.

According to the government, the amendments aim to improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, enhance consistency and improve transparency for patients and families. Those are worthy objectives. No reasonable person opposes a system that learns better and communicates better with the families who need to hear from it.

But legislation is not judged by its intentions. It is judged by its consequences.

So, before we create new structures or grant new powers, what specific problem is this bill trying to address? The Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews. What has failed? Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? These concerns were raised during the briefing on the bill, and rightfully so, because legislative changes ought to follow a demonstrated gap and the government has not put clear data in front of this House showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we are legislating in search of a problem. Diagnosis comes before treatment.

Bill 40 also creates a New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper that sounds fine. Who could oppose expert advice on patient safety?

Here is where we should slow down. Health care professionals in this province already operate within Horizon Health Network, Vitalite Health Network, professional regulatory colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees and patient advocacy offices, and every one of those structures generates paperwork that somebody in scrubs has to fill out at the end of a shift. Front-line workers are telling us they spend more time on forms than on patients. Are we improving outcomes, or are we adding bureaucracy? If this committee is one more reporting layer with nothing measurable behind it, we will have made the system worse. That is my worry.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls. It makes a difference. Today the program is with Horizon Health Network at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m., helping seniors set up access to MyHealthNB, the secure online portal where a person can look at their own blood work and their own imaging results. Hands-on help. A senior needs two things to walk in there and come out with an account: a Medicare card and an email address. That is it. Horizon staff verify identity on the spot and hand over the access code. No appointment. No registration. This is what breaking down a barrier looks like, and it is how seniors in our communities stay connected to their own health information and stay healthy and independent where they live. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the outstanding work of Nursing Home Without Walls. Today they are with Horizon Health Network at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby past the gift shop, from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. They are signing seniors up for MyHealthNB. A senior can sit down with someone there, get hands-on help, and reach the point of seeing their own blood work and their own imaging results, securely, on a screen. Bring a Medicare card and an email address. That is the whole list. Horizon staff verify identity and give out the access code right there — no appointment, no registration, nothing booked ahead. Nursing Home Without Walls has been taking barriers down like this in the lives of seniors in our communities for a while now, and seniors stay connected to their own health information, and stay healthy and independent, because of it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk — Indian Island First Nation — have written a cookbook, Mitji: Let's Eat! Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It is an exceptional cultural contribution and I want to congratulate them for it today. The book stands as a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. This is not just a cookbook. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, and the authors take on gastrocolonialism directly: colonial policy reached into the kitchen and altered what a traditional Indigenous recipe was permitted to be. My copy has a broken spine already. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.
