Madam Speaker, this bill does not approve anything. It makes things easier. It takes barriers out of the way, it says plainly what the rules are, and it puts New Brunswick in a position to move when the time comes. We drafted the proposal with the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, the Department of Indigenous Affairs, and others. The NB Power Board of Directors keeps oversight of every security measure, exactly as it does today; the board answers for the money and the board answers for the risk. What we gather becomes the proposal that goes to government for approval, and someone reviews it before anybody authorizes anything. The Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future. This bill makes sure we can meet what that project throws at us, bend where we need to bend, and know where we stand while we do it. I am asking members to support it so we can take the next step toward clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, my colleague across the way said a few minutes ago that this bill will "approve the Mactaquac project." That is not what is in front of us at second reading. The bill's aim is to make things easier, not to approve them. It removes barriers, it provides clarity, and it makes sure New Brunswick is prepared to move forward when the time comes. On the consultation point the member raised: the proposal was drafted with the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures — and "continue" is the word I want on the record, because financial accountability and risk mitigation do not move anywhere. The information will be used as the basis of the proposal submitted for government approval, and it will be reviewed before any authorization. The Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future, and this bill ensures we are prepared to meet its challenges with the flexibility, clarity, and confidence required. I urge all members to support the bill and take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, employees must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. They are required to inform the employer as soon as possible of their need for leave. Employers may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. Those elements support the integrity of the leave and give employers reasonable assurance and predictability. A member stopped me in the hallway this morning with three questions and I will put them on the record. What happens to a seasonal worker who is 80 days in? Who pays for the note from the doctor? Does a nurse practitioner's signature count as medical documentation? I don't have those answers today. This amendment strengthens protections for workers when they are most vulnerable, while keeping a balanced approach that considers the realities of workplaces across the province. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. It addresses a clear gap in our current legislation, and it keeps a reasonable, structured approach for employers. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. That might seem minor, but clarity matters. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at approved farmers' markets, something small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for. A microbrewery or a craft distillery that can sell straight to customers at the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen — the St. George one runs Saturday mornings — helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. It recognizes a sector that has truly taken off here in New Brunswick.

That said, modernization should never come without scrutiny. The caps are in the bill's own text: 500 000 L for brewers, 75 000 L for distillers, and that is when they are operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation. Put the two side by side. The brewers' ceiling is somewhere between six and a half and seven times the distillers'. And neither figure is set against anything — not against the agency limit that applies today, not against what the average craft producer in this province actually put out last year. The Corporation has those production numbers. This House does not.

So those sound like fair limits right up until you ask who they fit. Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers, or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier? We've seen well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays.

Craft producers in St. Croix, people who pour their life savings into starting a brewery or a distillery, say: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our government's economic development strategy has one priority: build a stronger and more competitive New Brunswick that gives people here somewhere to go.

New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. A company that grows, finds a buyer in a new market, and puts money back into its own plant hires people, and those people hold up the schools, the clinics, the roads, the rinks, and the ferry my constituents phone me about. That is the chain. It is not complicated.

The strategy builds on what we already do well. We want our firms to get more out of an hour of work, we want them trying things they haven't tried, and we want them able to sell into a global economy that will not sit still and wait for them. We are going after investment. We are backing defence and mining. We want the growth to outlast the people in this room.

Departments will work off one list of priorities and be measured against it. Ministers answer for that list.

The government cannot do this alone. We need industry, we need the universities and the colleges, we need communities across the province, and we need every member sitting in this House. The people we have shown it to so far like that it is short, that it says who does what, and that it says by when.

New Brunswick has what the world wants. We are competing to win, and when the economy grows there is more to pay for the services families rely on every single day. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new, hoped-for bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I want to talk about labour relations in New Brunswick. Workers make their living inside those relations, and the economy of this province grows or stalls with them, so this matters to everyone in this Chamber. Over the last few years the Higgs government and the labour movement have fallen into a troubling pattern. The government has not sat down with workers and their representatives to talk and to bargain. It has legislated instead. Bill 23 in 2022. Bill 17 last fall. The essential service legislation this House debated in December 2019. Three separate times, this government settled a labour question inside the Legislative Assembly rather than at a table with New Brunswick workers sitting across from it. It did not consult the unions properly and it did not work with them, and the distance between this government and the people who do the work has widened every time. Each one of those bills was a chance the government let go by. The amendments to the Public Service Labour Relations Act were a chance. The change to the essential service legislation was a chance. Employers and employees have to trust one another to get anything done, and this government has spent that trust down to very little. Workers across the province feel it. Nurses feel it, snowplow operators feel it, the people who answer the phones at Service New Brunswick feel it, and so do the folks in the yards in Edmundston. They are disillusioned. Morale in the workforce has dropped, and our industries are less productive and worse off for it.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour told this House a little while ago that his government has "a good working relationship" with organized labour. Those are the words I want to test, because labour relations decide whether workers in this province can make a living and whether our economy keeps growing. In recent years a troubling pattern has emerged between the Higgs government and the labour movement in New Brunswick. Instead of meeting workers and their representatives at the table, this government reaches for a bill. Bill 23, in 2022. Bill 17, last fall. The essential service legislation this House debated in December 2019. Three separate times, the matter was settled here, inside the Legislative Assembly, rather than through negotiation with New Brunswick workers. On none of those three were the unions adequately consulted. My colleague raised exactly that during second reading of Bill 17 and got no answer worth writing down. The amendments to the Public Service Labour Relations Act, and the change to the essential service legislation that the member opposite described at the time as tidying up, were opportunities to build trust with the labour movement, and this government let both of them go. Trust between employers and employees is what makes a workplace productive, and it has been eroded. Workers are disillusioned. Morale in the workforce has fallen, and our industries carry the cost of that.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association are in the gallery today, and several of them sit on the association's Board of Directors. A few of them travelled from as far as Bathurst to get here for two o'clock. Their work holds up mental health and well-being in this province. The association keeps working with the Department of Health, and our system of care is stronger for that. There is more to say about it, and I will say it later today. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, March gives us a chance to thank social workers and to say plainly how much their work matters in the lives of New Brunswickers. Social workers sit with people on the worst day of those people's lives. They advocate, they arrange care, they treat the person in front of them with respect, and they get results that show up years later in somebody's kitchen. They work in addictions and mental health, with children and youth in care, with seniors, with women and gender equity files, and in a fair number of places nobody thinks to list. Inside the Department of Social Development, over 600 social workers help New Brunswickers get long-term care and disability support, and they protect children and seniors from abuse. They stand behind foster families. They speak up for people who cannot speak up for themselves, and they make sure services actually arrive at the door. This National Social Work Month, we thank them for their compassion and for sticking with it, and for the difference they make to lives and to communities across New Brunswick. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities. I will be honest, I did not know this day existed until somebody in my office put it in front of me a few years back, and I have thought about it every December since. I want to recognize the strength, the contributions, and the resilience of persons with disabilities across New Brunswick. We are committed to a province where every person has an equal opportunity to take part fully in our communities, our schools, our workplaces, and our public spaces. This summer we acted on that. We made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit would not detract from provincial disability programs, so that federal programs complement provincial support rather than replace it. Is that enough on its own? No, and I would not stand here and say it is. Accessibility and inclusion are not optional. They are essential to true equity. Let us keep removing barriers so that every New Brunswicker can live, work, and thrive. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, today, on the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, we recognize the strength, the contributions, and the resilience of persons with disabilities across New Brunswick. The member opposite asked during question period whether federal money was going to be, and I am using her words, "quietly netted off" provincial programs. It was not. This summer we made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit would not detract from provincial disability programs, and federal programs will complement provincial support rather than replace it. That is the commitment, and members can hold me to it. We are building a province where every person has an equal opportunity to participate fully in our communities, our schools, our workplaces, and our public spaces. Accessibility and inclusion are not optional. They are essential to true equity. Let us keep working together to remove barriers and to make sure every New Brunswicker can live and work here without limits. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I learned this week that Roméo H. LeBlanc has died. He was 102. He was an Acadian, and he was a veteran of the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to him for his exceptional service to our country.

The war was not the end of it. For the decades after he came home he stayed with the veterans' community, showing up for the men and women who had served, and making sure that the ones who did not come back were still spoken about by name at the Legion and in his own town. Courage, devotion, a deep sense of duty. He had all of it, and he would have waved it off if you said so. He would have.

On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, his loved ones, and the entire veterans' community. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. As the holiday season comes on, I rise to talk about shopping local.

Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. They are the cafes and restaurants where neighbours gather, the boutiques and artisans that bring character to our downtowns, and the family-owned shops passed down through generations. They are the local producers who remind us that world-class quality is made right here at home. They are employers, they hold up their communities, and they are a real part of the economic development of this province.

When we choose to shop locally, particularly during the holidays, we are doing more than purchasing a gift. We are investing directly in our communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick, creating jobs, supporting local supply chains and strengthening our regional economies. Honestly, I'm not an economist, and I couldn't tell you the exact multiplier. I do know what it looks like on a main street when the money stays.

At the Premier's open house yesterday, the turnout was strong and the vendors were a genuinely varied bunch. I'll admit I went in expecting the same faces I always see. I was wrong. I spoke to one vendor who started his business at nine years old.

So go to the markets this holiday season. Visit a neighbourhood shop you have walked past for years. Find the artisans, and choose New Brunswick-made products and services where you can. The choices are small, and they add up, and by supporting local shopping we're supporting the people who support us all year.

A special thank-you to everyone who was out yesterday and who spoke to those vendors.

Madam Speaker, a new provincial website went live this week: artsculturenb.ca. It puts artists, artisans and the places you can go and see them in one spot, and it arrived just in time for the holiday season.

A New Brunswicker hunting for a gift can find one on it — a print, a concert ticket, a bowl, a Saturday market two towns over. Artists and organizations post their own events and their own work on the site themselves. Nobody has to ask us first.

We built it so that more people know what is being made here, get out to see it, and pay for it. I encourage everyone to visit artsculturenb.ca and see what this province is making.

This holiday season, let's encourage local shopping, celebrate our local talent, and support the artists who make our province extraordinary. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell is a powerful example of how one person can make a real difference in their community. In Little River, he has dedicated his time and energy to building a facility and small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who are often overlooked and forgotten. He saw his friends, as he always calls them, homeless on the streets of Moncton, and instead of turning away he chose to step up.

He provides necessities like food and clothing, but more importantly he offers dignity and hope. He reminds us that homelessness is not just an issue but a human experience, and that everyone deserves kindness and opportunity. His efforts bring the community together and pull other people in with him.

Change starts with one person choosing to care.

The last time I was out there, one of the little homes had a doorbell on it. A real doorbell, wired in. Somebody had put it there so people would knock. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. They'll be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into mere ornaments — sparkly, shiny, and completely hollow. First, there was the balanced budget promise, the one we were told would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. Now, I'm no accountant, and I won't pretend I've read every line of that budget. I know what the bottom line said. It's not even the gift that keeps on giving. It's the gift that keeps on taking. Then there's the carbon tax adjustor, a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. Well, it's still there, adding to the prices of everything we buy every day. I filled up in Sussex on Saturday and paid it. That's not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. New Brunswickers have been promised a lot of things. This government needs to realize that promises aren't just for the Christmas season. They're for the whole year. It's time they deliver.

Madam Speaker, each year, on November 11, we pause to remember the brave men and women who served and continue to serve our country in times of war, conflict, and peacekeeping. Their courage, sacrifice, and unwavering sense of duty have safeguarded the freedom and values we cherish today. We also pay tribute to the families who have carried the burden of separation and grief, and to the veterans who have returned home changed by their service — the families who carry that burden of separation and loss, and the veterans who came home forever changed. As we gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick, may we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget. I'll be at the cenotaph at eleven o'clock, in the cold, with my father's medals in my coat pocket.

Madam Speaker, on November 11 we stop and we remember the brave men and women who served this country and who serve it still — in war, in conflict, on peacekeeping duty. Their courage and their sacrifice, and a sense of duty they never once set down, safeguarded the freedom and the values we cherish today. Their families carried something too. They carried the separation and the grief. Veterans came home changed by their service, and some of them came home and did not say a word about it for forty years. We will gather at cenotaphs and memorials across New Brunswick — in Fredericton, in Bathurst, in Perth-Andover, at a stone in a field outside Doaktown — and there we renew our commitment to peace, to gratitude, and to never forgetting those who gave everything for Canada. Lest we forget. Lest we forget.

Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill, and that fee goes through Finance and Treasury Board. Property owners also pay charges through their local tax rates. So the same owner is paying twice, directly and indirectly. First, the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee printed on the tax bill. Second, the municipal taxes that are used to pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services.

Madam Speaker, most New Brunswickers do not know that. They look at the one visible charge on the bill and assume that is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize that the municipality is paying Service New Brunswick as well.

I want to be absolutely clear about something. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts. Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. Finance and Treasury Board is charging the cost of assessment fee directly through the property tax bill, and that is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate. After years of rising assessments and rising costs, the time has come to do it.

I brought my own notice with me. Mine went up somewhere around 11% to 12% in a single year, against 3% or so the year before that. That figure is off my kitchen table, not out of the department, and I would welcome the minister correcting it with the departmental number.

No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income requested that a modest house be reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know that assessments have gone up in recent years. With COVID-19 and people moving to New Brunswick, home prices went up, and fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process. That is why the increase was what it was. Every time an assessment rises, the government's revenue from this fee rises with it. That creates a perception, and it is a troubling one: that government benefits financially from the very increases that keep a woman on a fixed income awake at two in the morning.

Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill. That is through Finance and Treasury Board. They also pay charges through their local tax rates, which means the same property owner is paying twice over, once directly on the bill in front of them and once indirectly through the municipal taxes their town or their rural district collects and then hands to Service New Brunswick for assessment services. Both ways. Same person.

Madam Speaker, many New Brunswickers do not know this. They see the visible charge on the tax bill and they assume that is the entirety of the assessment cost. They do not realize the municipality is paying too.

Let me be clear. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and to rural districts, so nobody here should walk out of this Chamber telling assessors that their work is on trial.

But Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. It is charging the fee. That is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate, and after years of rising assessments and rising costs, I would argue the time has come to do it.

People feel the government benefits from circumstances they cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income asked to have a modest house reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know that assessments have gone up in recent years. With COVID-19, and with people moving here from away, home prices went up. Fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process, and that is why the increase was so sharp.

Up go the assessments. Up goes the revenue from this fee. That creates a perception, and the perception is that government does well out of the same increases that keep the rest of them up at night.

Mr. Speaker, labour relations in this province are in bad shape, and that hurts everybody who is trying to build something here. This government's legislative approach has fallen short, and we should say so. Going forward, we should talk to workers honestly, we should show them what we are doing, and we should treat their representatives as people we are dealing with rather than problems we are managing. Trust gets built that way. Nothing else builds it.

In December 2019, this Legislature was embroiled in a contentious debate over essential service legislation, and it was specifically about the wages of nursing home workers. Bill 17 imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on those wages. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions opposed the bill. They worried about what it would do to their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage, and they said so loudly.

The bill passed. Union leaders called it an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced, and she said they would keep fighting for better working conditions and for the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society.

Bill 17 showed how far apart this government and the unions had drifted on labour rights and on collective bargaining. It also showed how hard it is to weigh what a worker is owed against what a taxpayer pays and what the treasury can carry. Nobody in this Chamber has ever found that easy.

When we look back at December 2019, we cannot forget that there are members sitting on the government benches today who were opposed to that bill. They said it out loud. They said they would stand with labour movements as long as they could. That has changed today.

The strain on our labour relations has become undeniable, and it is casting a shadow over the collective effort to build prosperity in New Brunswick. I think this government's legislative approach has fallen short, and we ought to acknowledge that. Going forward, we should prioritize genuine dialogue, transparency, and mutual respect in our dealings with workers and their representatives. Trust is built that way or it is not built at all.

Mr. Speaker, in December 2019, this Legislature was embroiled in a contentious debate over essential service legislation, specifically about the wages of nursing home workers. Honestly, I am not an arbitrator and I have never sat at a bargaining table, so I will not pretend to know the mechanics of it better than the people who lived it. What I do know is that Bill 17 imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on the wages of these workers, and that members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions voiced their opposition and expressed their concern about the impact on their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage. Their protest underscored the depth of their discontent.

The law passed. Union leaders decried it as an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced, and she emphasized their commitment to fighting for better working conditions and to protecting the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society. I have read her remarks. I would not want to be on the other side of them.

Bill 17 highlighted the ongoing tension between the government and labour unions in this province, particularly on labour rights and collective bargaining. It underscored the challenge in balancing the interests of workers against those of taxpayers and against the government's fiscal responsibility. I do not know where the line sits. I am not sure anyone in here does.

But when we reflect on December 2019 and the passage of Bill 17, we cannot forget that there are members of this government today who were opposed to that bill. They vocally expressed their discontent. They said they would stand with labour movements as long as they could. That has changed today.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the battle in 2027.

My colleague from across the floor said last week that we are "a country that forgets too easily." I do not think he is wrong. That is what Vimy Week is for, and it runs this year from April 2 to April 9.

I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. The pin is composed of four distinct colours, and it symbolizes the unity and the sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. I have pins here with me, and I will pass them to both sides of the Chamber before we rise.

By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice, and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, on October 24, in Newtown, we marked the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson. Laura is strong, she is vibrant, and she is still living independently in her own home. She held a valid driver's licence until just this past month, which is a bit over 88 years after she got her first one, and she was still taking short drives on the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were true pioneers in this province's agricultural and tourism sectors. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick, and that museum has done as much as any body in this province to preserve our farming heritage. In 1967, Canada's centennial year, they opened New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience. Families and travellers came from across the province and from around the world, and they kept coming for decades. Laura still shares her humour, her stories and her advice, whether or not you asked for it. Congratulations on 105 years, Laura, and thank you.

Madam Speaker, on October 24, Newtown celebrated Laura Anderson's 105th birthday. Laura is remarkable — strong, vibrant, and still living independently in her own home. She kept her driver's licence until just this past month and took short drives on the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were true pioneers in New Brunswick's agricultural and tourism sectors. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick. In 1967, they launched New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience, and people came from across the province and from around the world to stay with them. There was a Jersey cow in that operation named Bessie, and I am told half the guests remember her better than they remember the farmhouse. Laura still tells the stories. She still has the humour, and she still has the wisdom, and she is happy to share both. We congratulate her on 105 remarkable years and thank her for what she has given this province.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. I can tell members what is actually on the tables every morning: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, cheese, and, at one school I visited, a toaster that has already been replaced twice. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy food, often bought from farms and businesses in their own area. Parents tell me the program saves them time and money. It takes the fight out of the morning. A child who has eaten will sit down and work; a child who has not will not, and every teacher in this House knows it. For many families, with the cost of living where it is, this is making a real difference. It is a concrete investment in our young people. Every child deserves to start the day on the right foot. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget, a historic budget of $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year. It is the largest capital budget that has ever been tabled in our province. The member opposite said yesterday that this is "money out the door with no plan." Those were his words, and I would ask him to look at where the money actually goes. Most of the investment is allocated to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure, to improve our roads, bridges, ferries and other essential infrastructure. The health care sector will also see significant investment, to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate our hospitals. In education, the capital budget includes building new schools in Shediac and Moncton and upgrading several institutions elsewhere in the province. When the capital estimates come before the Committee of Supply, the member can put every one of those lines to the minister, item by item. These investments are essential to deal with the backlog caused by years of underinvestment. They show our commitment to safety, to quality of life and to the future of our communities. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I'll be honest with the House — I am not a transportation planner, and I had to go back and read the 2017 report again before I put this motion on the order paper. From Surfaces to Services. It said this province needed a comprehensive, coordinated approach to public transportation. That was 2017. Nothing meaningful has been done since.

Whose desk is it on? I don't know. That is the whole problem. Nobody owns the file, so nobody answers for it. Give one minister a mandate and somebody has to answer for the leadership, the coordination, the money, the way the pieces connect, and the schedules that never line up.

Be it therefore resolved that this Legislative Assembly urge the Premier to give the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure a mandate for public transportation; and be it further resolved that this Assembly urge government to allocate the resources and the funding the New Brunswick Transportation Authority needs to create a public transportation strategy and to implement it.

Madam Speaker, I want to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls, which keeps making a real difference for seniors in our communities. Today it is partnering with Horizon Health Network to give seniors hands-on assistance setting up access to MyHealthNB, a secure online portal that lets a person look up their own blood work and their own imaging results rather than waiting on a call back from somebody's office. Staff are there now. They are at the Miramichi Regional Hospital, in the main lobby, today from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Bring a Medicare card and an email address. That is all it takes to create an account. Horizon staff verify identity and hand over the access code on the spot, and there is no appointment and no registration needed. This is how a barrier comes down. Seniors stay connected to their own health information, and they stay healthy and independent. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I'd like to recognize the work of Nursing Home Without Walls, which continues to make a real difference in the lives of seniors in our communities. A senior who does this today will not have to phone anybody to find out their own results. Main lobby, Miramichi Regional Hospital, until 2 p.m. Bring the card. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to congratulate Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk on their recent cookbook, Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It stands as a testament to the rich heritage and resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. Mr. Speaker, this is not just a cookbook. The recipes are enriched with the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations. The authors take on gastrocolonialism directly — colonial policy changed what people could cook, and it altered traditional Indigenous recipes. My copy is in the kitchen at home, next to my mother's old Purity cookbook, which is where a cookbook belongs. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions. Wela'lin.

Mr. Speaker, today I want to congratulate two remarkable authors, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, on their recent cookbook, Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. It is a testament to the rich heritage and the resilient spirit of the people of Mi'gma'gi. This is not just a cookbook, Mr. Speaker. The recipes carry the historical knowledge and the lived experience of a community that has thrived on these lands for generations, and the authors do not stop at the food — they address the profound impacts of gastrocolonialism, which is to say how colonial policies altered traditional Indigenous recipes. That took work. Mr. Speaker, I invite all members to join me in congratulating Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck for their commitment to preserving Indigenous culinary traditions.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to congratulate two remarkable authors, Margaret Augustine and Lauren Beck of L'nui Menikuk, also known as Indian Island First Nation, on their recent cookbook, Mitji— Let's Eat!: Mi'kmaq Recipes from Sikniktuk. This bill does not approve anything. It makes things easier. It takes barriers out of the way so that New Brunswick can move when the time comes, and it says plainly what has to happen first. We drafted it with several departments at the table: the Office of the Attorney General, Service New Brunswick, the Department of Post-Secondary Education, Training and Labour, and the Department of Indigenous Affairs. The NB Power Board of Directors will continue to oversee all security measures, so the board, and not this Chamber, answers for the money and for the risk. What comes out of that work becomes the basis of the proposal that goes to government for approval, and government reviews it before it authorizes anything at all. Madam Speaker, the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future. This bill makes sure we are ready when the challenges land, with room to move and a clear path to follow. I urge all members of the House to support the bill and help us take the next step toward securing clean energy for New Brunswickers, today and for decades to come. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The bill on long-term illness and injury leave protects workers, and it is an essential step forward. A person who gets sick should not have to pick between getting better and paying the mortgage. Again, Madam Speaker, this is not an ordinary bill. It is a concrete commitment to our people. A worker can take up to 27 weeks of protected leave and come back to the same position or an equivalent job. That means the employer holds the spot, the family keeps the paycheque coming as best it can, and nobody comes back to find their name off the schedule. The bill updates our employment standards so they match how people actually live: a diagnosis, a treatment schedule, a spouse doing the driving, a kid who still has to get to school. Madam Speaker, we bring in legislation like this to stand behind people when they are sick, when they are hurting, and when they are being treated unfairly. These are not housekeeping measures.

Employees must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. The member opposite asked me during second reading what "as soon as possible" means in practice. It means what it says: the employee informs the employer as soon as possible of their need for leave. My colleague also pressed on the word "reasonable." Employers may require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury — reasonable, not a weekly note. These elements support the integrity of the leave while giving employers assurance and predictability, and members can test them clause by clause when this amendment to the Employment Standards Act goes to the Standing Committee on Economic Policy. Madam Speaker, this amendment strengthens protections for workers at a time when they are most vulnerable, while keeping a balanced approach that considers the realities of workplaces across the province. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. This amendment addresses a clear gap in our current legislation. It is a practical and necessary step. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Employees must have at least 90 days of continuous employment to be eligible for the leave, which aligns with leave provisions in other provinces. Employees are required to inform their employer as soon as possible of their need for leave. Employers may also require reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee is unable to work due to illness or injury. That is not a hurdle. It gives an employer some assurance and some predictability about who is coming back and when, and it keeps the leave from being something other than what this House intended it to be. Madam Speaker, this amendment is an important step forward. It strengthens protections for workers at a time when they are most vulnerable, and it does that while taking account of what workplaces across this province actually look like — a garage with four employees, a call centre with four hundred, a farm where the season does not wait for anybody's recovery. New Brunswick should be a place where people can live and work with dignity. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. This amendment addresses a clear gap in our legislation. It is a practical step. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

An employee must have worked 90 days in a row to be eligible for this leave, and that matches what other provinces do. The employee tells the employer as soon as they can that they need the leave. The employer may ask for reasonable medical documentation confirming that the employee cannot work because of illness or injury. Those two requirements keep the leave doing what it is supposed to do, and they let an employer plan. Madam Speaker, this amendment is an important step forward. It protects workers when they are at their most vulnerable, and it does not ignore what employers are up against in shops, offices, plants, kitchens, and one-truck operations in rural New Brunswick. A person should be able to live here, work here, and keep their dignity while doing it. No one should have to choose between their health and their job. Our current legislation leaves a gap, and this amendment closes it. A worker who is sick keeps the job. An employer knows where things stand. Thank you very much, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the minister's statement on the InnovateNB Awards. It is an occasion to celebrate the people who are pushing boundaries and driving progress in New Brunswick, and I congratulate this year's recipients. But no innovator works in a vacuum. Someone has to build the ecosystem around them, and this province still puts barriers in the way of people who are trying. The minister told the House that businesses have a growing confidence in New Brunswick's climate. Not every business shares it. A machine shop in Doaktown, a software firm in Moncton, a boat builder on the Acadian Peninsula, a woodlot operator, a nurse practitioner running her own clinic — they do not all get at the same programs on the same terms. Rural applicants cannot reach the resources and the supports that people in the urban centres reach. Innovation has to pay off in every corner of this province, not only for the people who already know whom to call. This year's recipients inspire me. But who is coming after them? We equip our youth by funding schools, by pairing them with mentors, and by opening funds they can actually get at. And the departments have to keep putting money into research and development, particularly in clean technology and sustainable practices, which is where our economic goals point. Let government, industry, and communities do this together, and let us leave nobody out. Our future depends on it. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

I want to start by recognizing that this bill brings forward some long-overdue clarifications. It updates outdated language, replacing legal Latin with plain English. Honestly, I'm not a lawyer, and I had a good chunk of this bill explained to me twice. That might seem minor, but clarity matters — and if it takes me two readings, imagine what it takes somebody who is running a still and filing the paperwork at the same time. It also simplifies the processes for brewers and distillers to sell their products at approved farmers' markets, something that small producers in New Brunswick have been asking for. The ability of a microbrewery or craft distillery to connect directly with customers at a local market, whether it's the Saint Andrews farmers' market, the St. George market, or the market in St. Stephen, helps drive tourism, encourages entrepreneurship, and strengthens local economies. I applaud that part of the bill, Madam Speaker. It recognizes the growth of a sector that has truly taken off here in New Brunswick. That said, modernization should never come without scrutiny. This bill sets production caps for breweries and distilleries operating as agents under the New Brunswick Liquor Corporation: 500 000 L for brewers, and 75 000 L for distillers. Now, those sound like fair limits to me. I don't know the industry well enough to say whether they are. So we need to ask: Were these caps determined in consultation with our smaller producers or primarily with larger operators? Will this inadvertently favour those already established in the market, making it harder for start-ups to grow into the next tier? We've seen this before, where well-intentioned changes to regulation end up benefitting those with deeper pockets and more connections, while small business owners struggle with compliance costs and licencing delays. I sat in a garage in St. Croix in February with a couple who had put their savings into a distillery, and they told me: We don't mind rules, but we just want fair ones. Craft producers elsewhere in New Brunswick say the same thing. This is my question for the government: How will fairness between small and large producers be ensured under this new licencing model?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our government's economic development strategy has one priority: a stronger, more competitive New Brunswick that gives the people who live here opportunities. New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. When a company grows, reaches new markets, and puts money back into its operations, it hires people, it holds a community together, and it pays for the public services families rely on every single day. The strategy builds on what we already have. We want our companies to be more productive, we want them to innovate, and we want them to win against anybody in a global economy that changes month to month. We will keep chasing investment. We will keep pushing on defence and mining. We will keep building for the long term. Departments will work off the same list of priorities and be measured against the same outcomes. The government cannot do this alone. We need industry, we need the universities and the community colleges, we need towns and villages across the province, and we need every member in this House. Stakeholders have told us early on that they like what they see: we have been clear, we have held the line, and we have shown them results. New Brunswick has what the world wants. We are competing to win, so that businesses can grow, communities can thrive, and opportunities open up across the province. When our economy grows, we can pay for better services and a more prosperous future for all New Brunswickers. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today with great satisfaction and deep gratitude. After years of waiting, the new, hoped-for bridge between Île Lamèque and Shippagan will be built. I thank the Premier, Hon. Susan Holt, and the Minister of Transportation and Infrastructure, Hon. Chuck Chiasson, for coming to the region in February and making that announcement, which marks a turning point for our communities. On behalf of my constituents, I want to express our gratitude to everyone who played a role in making this important project for our community happen. There was a man at the announcement in February with a photo of the old bridge in his coat pocket. He'd been carrying it around for years. He didn't say anything. He just showed it to me. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I'm pleased to welcome members of the New Brunswick Psychiatric Association who are with us in the gallery, and among them members of the association's Board of Directors. I'm not a clinician and I won't pretend to understand the half of what they do in a day. I do know their work is essential to supporting New Brunswickers' mental health and well-being. Madam Speaker, the month of March gives us an opportunity to pay tribute to social workers and to recognize the considerable importance of their work in New Brunswickers' lives. Offering care, advocacy, and support with empathy and respect, social workers are a source of healing, resilience, and hope. They transform lives and uplift communities with their dedication to dignity and human rights. Social workers play vital roles across many sectors, including addictions and mental health, children and youth in care, seniors, and women and gender equity. Within the Department of Social Development, over 600 social workers help New Brunswickers access long-term care and disability support and help protect children and seniors from abuse. They support foster families, advocate for vulnerable individuals, and ensure that vital services reach those in need. This National Social Work Month, we thank them for their compassion and their commitment to improving lives across New Brunswick. One of them, in Bathurst, spent last Thursday afternoon on the phone finding a bed for a man who had been sleeping in a stairwell. She found one. That is the job. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

The bill empowers the minister to require health care organizations to implement improvement plans. Accountability matters, and I'm not going to stand here and argue against it. What worries me is centralization. Health care organizations operate in vastly different environments, such as urban hospitals, rural facilities, community clinics, and long-term care settings. A one-size-fits-all approach imposed from the centre may not reflect local realities. In Perth-Andover the nurse practitioner covers three villages and does her own scheduling; a plan written on Queen Street will not know that. Ministerial authority should support improvement rather than replace professional judgment. Oversight should guide, not micromanage.

Perhaps the most serious issue lies in subsection 6.2. It says that if the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act prevails. That is a significant legal step. Government members are effectively creating an exception to one of the most core privacy protections governing public institutions. I am not a lawyer, and I would welcome being told I have this wrong. But I read subsection 6.2 four times last night and that is what it says.

The government argues that confidentiality encourages open discussion during safety reviews. There is merit to that. Health care professionals must feel safe speaking candidly. Overriding existing privacy legislation still demands rigorous justification. What could be withheld, from whom, with what appeal? Too much secrecy undermines public trust. Too little discourages honest reporting. This clause deserves detailed committee scrutiny.

The bill also expands rules allowing the disclosure of incident reports and improvement findings. System-wide learning is a good objective. Disclosure frameworks still have to protect patient identity. My fear is that information flows upward into bureaucracy and never reaches the front-line practitioners who could prevent the next one. Learning has to travel across the system, not just up into reports.

One theme runs through the bill: administration. New committees, new reporting obligations, new procedural requirements. Administration is not inherently negative. But every hour spent preparing reports is an hour not spent with patients, and the government has to show these additions will measurably improve care outcomes. Otherwise we are adding weight to a system already struggling.

Madam Speaker, today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, and we recognize the strength, contributions, and resilience of persons with disabilities across New Brunswick. The member for Fredericton South asked in this House last month whether the province intended to "offset" the federal benefit. She used that word, and I want to answer it plainly. This summer we made sure the federal Canada Disability Benefit wouldn't detract from provincial disability programs. No offset. Federal programs are to complement provincial support, not replace it. We remain committed to a province where every person has an equal opportunity to participate fully in our communities, schools, workplaces, and public spaces. Accessibility and inclusion are not optional. They are essential to true equity. Let us keep working together to remove barriers, promote dignity, and ensure that every New Brunswicker can live, work, and thrive without limitations. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Roméo H. LeBlanc has died at the age of 102. He was an Acadian, and he served in the Second World War. As Minister responsible for Military Affairs, I want to pay tribute to a man who gave this country exceptional service. Mr. LeBlanc did not stop when the war ended. He spent the rest of his life with the veterans' community — visiting them, sitting on committees, chasing down names, photographs, service records, the odd letter home — so that the men and women who served would not be forgotten. He was a courageous man and a dutiful one, and young people who come across his story will be the better for it. On behalf of the government of New Brunswick, I extend my sincerest condolences to his family, to those who loved him, and to the veterans who knew him. We will remember him. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. The holiday season is nearly here, and I rise to talk about supporting our local businesses at the time of year when our communities are shining brighter than ever. Small businesses are the heartbeat of New Brunswick's economy. I mean the cafes and restaurants where neighbours gather, the boutiques and artisans that give our downtowns their character, the family-owned shops passed down through generations, and the local producers who remind us that world-class quality is made right here at home. They are not only storefronts. They are employers, they support their communities, and they are essential contributors to the economic development of this province.

When we choose to shop locally, particularly during the holidays, we are doing more than purchasing a gift. We are investing directly in our communities. For every dollar spent locally, more of that dollar stays right here in New Brunswick, creating jobs, supporting local supply chains and strengthening our regional economies. I'm not an economist, and I'm not going to stand here and put a number on that multiplier. But I saw the thing itself yesterday at the Premier's open house. So many vendors, and such a range of them. I spoke with one man who started his business when he was nine years old. Nine.

Well, that turnout told me two things. New Brunswickers want to buy local. And the talent in our small business community is remarkable. I encourage everyone to get out to the markets this season, visit the neighbourhood shops, find the artisans, and choose New Brunswick-made products and services. Choices big and small make a real difference, especially at this time of year. When we support local, we support the people who support us all year. I want to thank everyone who was out yesterday and took the time to speak with those vendors.

Madam Speaker, we have launched a new provincial website for the arts in New Brunswick. It is called artsculturenb.ca, and it is up just in time for the holiday season. The site puts our artists and artisans in front of the people looking for them — potters, fiddlers, weavers, glassblowers, and whoever is running the craft table at a church basement sale in December. A New Brunswicker can use it to find a gift nobody else will be giving, or a concert, or a show. That money goes to our creative sector and to the people in it, who do a great deal for the communities they live in. Anyone working in arts and culture can put their own events and their own work up on the site themselves. Go and look at artsculturenb.ca. Shop local this holiday season, and buy from the person who made the thing. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, Charlie Burrell shows what one person can do in a community. In Little River, he has put his own time and his own energy into a facility and into small homes for people experiencing homelessness — people who get overlooked and forgotten. He saw his friends, as he always calls them, on the streets of Moncton. He did not turn away. He stepped up. He brings food and clothing out to them, and more than that, he brings dignity and he brings hope. Homelessness is not a file. It is happening to people, and everyone deserves kindness and an opportunity. Charlie has pulled others in with him, and the community shows up now because he does. Change starts with one person choosing to care. Thank you, Charlie. You care so much.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. I rise today in sadness on the passing of Robert Hosford. He was a husband, a father, a pop pop, an uncle, a great-uncle and a friend, and he died on Wednesday, November 12. Robert loved his people, he made them laugh, and he took them along on whatever he was doing next. He was the cornerstone of that family and he put what they needed ahead of what he needed. There was no limit to it. If you needed a hand, Robert gave you one. If you needed someone to listen, he sat down and listened. That warm smile could light up a room, and so could the laugh. He could turn the toughest day into a day somebody remembers. Robert was his family's biggest cheerleader, proud of what they took on and loud about what they pulled off. He loved his teams, and he loved teaching a lesson, and only his family came ahead of that. Please join me in expressing condolences to Robert's family and his friends. Thank you.

As New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they'll be exchanging more than just presents. They'll be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into mere ornaments — sparkly, shiny, and completely hollow. Hollow. I'll say that one again: completely hollow. First, there was the balanced budget promise, the one we were told would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. It's not even the gift that keeps on giving. It's the gift that keeps on taking. Then there's the carbon tax adjustor — a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. With the stroke of a pen. That's all it needed. Instead, it's still there, still adding to the prices of everything we buy every day. That's not the Christmas cheer we were hoping for. New Brunswickers have been promised a lot of things. This government needs to realize that promises aren't just for the Christmas season. They're for the whole year. It's time they deliver.
