Property owners pay the cost of assessment fee on the property tax bill, which is through Finance and Treasury Board. But they also pay charges through their local tax rates. So the same property owner is paying twice: directly, through the Finance and Treasury Board cost of assessment fee on the tax bill, and indirectly, through the municipal taxes that the municipality uses to pay Service New Brunswick for assessment services.

Madam Speaker, I'll be honest — I did not understand this myself until I went looking, and I am not an accountant. Most New Brunswickers don't know it either. They assume the visible charge on the bill is the whole assessment cost. They don't realize municipalities are paying Service New Brunswick as well.

I want to be absolutely clear about something. This motion does not criticize the work performed by Service New Brunswick. Assessment services are necessary. Municipalities require accurate assessments. The assessment system matters, and Service New Brunswick provides an actual service to municipalities and rural districts. But Finance and Treasury Board is not providing assessment services. Finance and Treasury Board is charging the cost of assessment fee directly through property tax bills. That is the charge this motion seeks to eliminate, and after years of rising assessments and rising costs, I would argue the time has come to do it.

People increasingly feel that the government financially benefits from circumstances ordinary citizens cannot control. No homeowner asked for property values to surge. No senior on a fixed income asked to have her modest home reassessed at a dramatically higher value, and we all know — we all know — that assessments have gone up in recent years. As I mentioned previously, with COVID-19 and people moving to New Brunswick, home prices went up. Fair market value is a big factor in the assessment process, and that's why the increase was what it was. I don't know where it stops. Every time those assessments rise, government revenue from this fee rises too. That creates a very troubling perception: that government benefits financially from the same assessment increases that cause property owners stress and anxiety.

Mr. Speaker, our labour relations are in bad shape, and that hangs over every effort we make together to build prosperity in New Brunswick. This government's legislative approach has fallen short, and we should say so. Going forward, talk to workers and their representatives honestly, show them the books, treat them decently. Trust gets built that way or not at all.

In December 2019, this Legislature fought over the essential service legislation, which was specifically focused on the wages of nursing home workers. Bill 17 imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on those wages, and it set off an intense reaction. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions came out against it. They said it would hurt their ability to strike and to negotiate a fair wage. You could hear how deep the discontent ran. The law passed anyway, and union leaders called it what they thought it was: an attack on public-sector labour unions. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced. She said they would keep fighting for better working conditions and for the rights of nursing home workers, who play a valuable role in our society.

Bill 17 showed how much tension sits between this government and the unions, particularly over labour rights and collective bargaining. It also showed how hard it is to balance what workers need against what taxpayers pay and what the government owes its own books.

When we look back at December 2019 and the passage of Bill 17, we can't forget that some of the people sitting on the government benches today were against that bill. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with labour movements as long as they could. That has changed today.

Madam Speaker, I rise to recognize the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. A member opposite said earlier this session that these commemorations amount to "a pin and a paragraph." I wrote it down at the time. I would ask that member to look at what the Vimy Foundation has done since 2006, which is to raise awareness and educate Canadians about that battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 2027, a milestone moment in Canada's history. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9. I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. That is what the colours are. It is not decoration. My colleague across the floor wore hers every sitting day last April, and I would ask the rest of us to do the same. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead-up to the 110th anniversary of the battle in 2027, a milestone moment in Canada's history. Vimy Week runs from April 2 to 9, and I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. It is composed of four distinct colours, one for each of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. By wearing it we honour their courage and their sacrifice and the legacy they left behind. The pin itself is smaller than a dime. Most of them end up in a desk drawer by May. Wear it anyway.

Madam Speaker, on October 24 our community celebrated the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson of Newtown. Laura is strong, she is vibrant, and she is still proudly living independently in her own home. Until just this past month she had kept her driver's licence and taken short drives through the rural roads she knows so well. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were true pioneers in New Brunswick's agricultural and tourism sectors. They were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick, and they helped preserve our province's rich farming heritage. In 1967 they launched New Brunswick's very first farm vacation experience. Families came from Saint John, from Maine, from Ontario, from Germany, and one summer from New Zealand. Laura still tells the stories, still remembers the names, and still laughs at the parts you would think she would be tired of by now. We congratulate her on 105 remarkable years and thank her for her contributions to our province. Thomas would have been ninety-eight this year.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. Every morning, throughout the province, students start their day with a nutritious meal: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. I am not a nutritionist. I could not tell you the protein numbers if a member asked me for them. What I can tell you is what I saw at a school in my riding in February, when a Grade 3 boy took a second bagel and put it in his coat pocket for later. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy foods, which are often sourced from our local farms and businesses. For many families, with the cost of living where it is, this program is making a real difference. It saves parents time and money and it reduces stress in the morning routine. And it means students come to class prepared to learn and able to concentrate. I do not know how you measure that last part. I know what the teachers tell me.

Madam Speaker, last September our government launched a universal breakfast program in all New Brunswick schools. Not some schools. I will say that again: all New Brunswick schools. Close to a year later, we are already seeing concrete results. Every morning, throughout the province, students start their day with a nutritious meal: milk, eggs, bagels, apples, and cheese. Through our partnership with FeedNB, schools are able to offer healthy foods, which are often sourced from our local farms and businesses. For many families, especially with the rising cost of living, this program is making a real difference. It saves parents time and money and reduces stress in their morning routine. And it means students come to class prepared to learn. That is the whole point of it, and I am going to repeat it because it gets lost in the arguing about the cost: students come to class prepared to learn. Every child deserves to start their day on the right foot, Madam Speaker. Thank you.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget, a historic budget of $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year. This is the largest capital budget ever tabled in our province. Most of the money goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure: roads, bridges, ferries, wharves, culverts, and the salt sheds nobody thinks about until February. The health care sector will also see significant investments, to modernize our medical equipment and renovate our hospitals. In education, the capital budget builds new schools in Shediac and Moncton and upgrades several institutions elsewhere in the province. Crews cannot pave a road that was never budgeted for, and that is the backlog years of underinvestment left us. Children will be safer walking to those schools. Their parents will get to work without losing a rim on Route 11. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, our government has presented the 2026-27 capital budget. It is $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year. That is the largest capital budget ever tabled in this province. Most of the investments will go to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure to improve our roads, bridges, ferries and other essential infrastructure, and the health care sector will also see significant investments, both to modernize our medical equipment and to renovate hospitals that in some cases have not had serious work done on them in my lifetime. In education, the budget builds new schools in Shediac and Moncton. It upgrades several institutions elsewhere in the province. This is not extravagance. It is the backlog left by years of underinvestment, and it has to be paid down eventually. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Deputy Speaker, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. Taking them to court and suggesting that they relocate to Alberta for better wages was not only a failure in negotiation but a betrayal of the individuals who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. I was not in the room for those talks. I have read the filings and I have spoken with two workers from the home in my riding, and that is the extent of what I know first-hand. One of them, a personal support worker with 22 years in, told me she had already looked up the flights. Then there was the 16-day school strike and the subsequent use of emergency orders to force workers back to work, which raised real questions about this government's commitment to meaningful dialogue and to the right to strike. Watering down binding arbitration, introducing scab-friendly legislation, and now this pension bill: the pattern erodes the foundation of workers' rights. I am not a labour lawyer. I do not know whether the arbitration change would survive a court challenge and I will not pretend that I do. What I do know is that the decisions made in this building land on the livelihoods of countless individuals and on the health of our communities. You will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate, the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements. I have never had a better line handed to me, and I did not write it.

So the province keeps its own veterinarians on the files only the province can handle, and private clinics take the routine calls. We are not walking away. We are building the model that most of the country already runs, so a farmer can still get a vet out to the barn this year and in ten years. New Brunswick can shape it around what farms here actually need and still hold the quality up.

I know the rollout is worrying people. Up in Restigouche, out on the Acadian Peninsula, past Plaster Rock, getting a vet to the door was already hard, and now producers are asking what it will cost and who will come. That is why we are putting together a support program for private-sector veterinarians. Part of it is meant to cover costs like travel, so a producer four hours from a clinic can still get the visit.

I would not tell you the answers we have given have settled anybody's mind. They have not. What they show is that we mean to find something that works farm by farm.

The labs are a piece of this too. They are the ones who catch a new disease early, before it moves through a herd, and they do the food-safety testing a processor cannot ship without. Through the transition, the existing labs stay open and stay staffed. Nobody's samples sit in a queue somewhere.

We need people onside for this. I want to hear from the producers, from the vets, from the people who have written to my office and told me flatly that they think we are wrong. We can get the money side and the quality side right at once. It is a big change and it only works if people come to it willing.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Well, I should say at the start that I am not an epidemiologist and I have not read every line of the Public Health Act. I have read the parts my staff flagged for me. That is honest.

But I lived through the same three years everybody in this Chamber did, and I saw what the pandemic did to our communities, our families, and our economy. So I am proposing a resolution calling on the government to take immediate action, before the next one.

Here is what I do understand. The Act is the cornerstone of the province's response and it is badly out of date. It says nothing about RSV. There is no mechanism in it for Public Health to add an illness to the ones it tracks — I asked about that in November and the letter I got back did not answer the question.

Now, readiness costs money: public health infrastructure, resources, personnel. I don't know what the number is. I know we did not have enough nurses in 2020 and I know we have fewer now.

And the response has to reach the people it missed. Seniors, people with underlying conditions, marginalized communities — they were hit hardest, and a strategy has to be built for their circumstances or it is not a strategy. My own mother waited nine days for a result in Fredericton, and she has a family doctor. Think about somebody who doesn't.

We should also be running education and awareness campaigns now, while nobody is frightened, because that is when people actually listen.

I ask all members to support the resolution.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act. That Act already sets up a framework for reviewing patient safety incidents and learning from them. The government says the amendments will improve how health care incidents are reviewed, strengthen collaboration, make reviews more consistent, and improve transparency for patients and families. Nobody is going to stand up and oppose that. But a bill is not judged by what it intends. It is judged by what it does.

So I want to put some questions to the minister. What specific problem is this bill trying to fix? Are incident reviews not happening now? Are the lessons not being shared? Are patients not being told? Are the health authorities ignoring recommendations? We raised this at the briefing on the bill. Those answers are not clearly provided.

Legislative change should follow a demonstrated gap. The government has not put forward data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we are legislating in search of a problem rather than solving one. Diagnosis before treatment.

The biggest change here is a new body, the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper, who could oppose expert advice on patient safety? Here is where I would slow down. Health care professionals in this province already answer to Horizon Health Network, Vitalité Health Network, professional regulatory colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees, and patient advocacy offices. Is this improving outcomes? Is it another layer? Which of those bodies gets wound up when this one starts? I don't know. Front-line workers already tell us they spend more and more of the day filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this committee becomes one more reporting layer with no measurable improvement, we will have worsened the very system we set out to help.

Bill 40 amends the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act, an Act that already tells hospitals how to review a patient safety incident and what to do with what they learn. The government says the amendments will improve how incidents get reviewed, strengthen collaboration, make reviews more consistent, and tell patients and families more. Nobody opposes any of that. But a bill does what it does, not what it means to do.

So what has failed? The Act is on the books already. Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? Are health authorities ignoring recommendations? Members raised all four at the briefing on the bill, and rightly so. The government has shown us no data pointing to a systemic failure under the current law. Change the law after you find the gap, not before. A doctor diagnoses before treating.

The biggest thing in the bill is a new committee, the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, which the minister sets up and keeps running. Fine, on paper. Who turns down expert advice on patient safety?

Slow down here. A nurse in Miramichi already answers to Horizon Health Network, a professional regulatory college, an accreditation body, an internal quality review committee, and a patient advocacy office. A nurse an hour west answers to Vitalité Health Network instead. That is five desks before this bill adds a sixth. Are we improving outcomes or adding bureaucracy? Front-line workers keep telling us they fill out forms in the hours they used to spend with patients. Add a reporting layer that improves nothing anyone can measure and you have worsened the very system you set out to help.

Thank you, Madam Speaker. Our government's economic development strategy is focused on one priority: building a stronger and more competitive New Brunswick that is a source of opportunity for people in this province. New Brunswick succeeds when our businesses succeed. A company that grows, reaches a new market, or invests in its own operations hires people, and those wages pay for the public services families rely on every single day.

The strategy builds on our existing strengths. It focuses on improving productivity, supporting innovation, and helping New Brunswick companies compete in a global economy that changes month to month. It reinforces our commitment to attracting investment, to strengthening key sectors such as defence and mining, and to long-term sustainable growth.

Productivity is where the gap sits. Statistics Canada has this province's output per hour below the national figure, and it was below it a decade ago too. That is the number I want moving, and I want it measured against Nova Scotia's, not against our own past. Defence and mining are two sectors, not twelve. We named two because a province this size that names twelve has named none.

We are taking a coordinated and accountable approach that brings departments together around shared priorities and outcomes somebody can actually measure. This is not work the government can do alone. It needs industry, the universities and the colleges, communities, and every member of this House. Early feedback from stakeholders has been positive, and what they keep naming back to us is our focus on clarity, discipline, and results.

New Brunswick has what the world wants. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

The bill lets the minister require a health care organization to put an improvement plan in place. Accountability matters. I don't quarrel with that. What worries me is the centre deciding for everybody. A hospital in Saint John, a clinic in Neguac, and a nursing home are not running the same problem, and a plan written downtown may not fit any of them. I want the minister's authority to back up professional judgment, not stand in for it.

The part that concerns me most is subsection 6.2. If the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act prevails. That is a serious legal step. We are carving an exception out of one of the core privacy protections that govern public institutions. The government says confidentiality gets people talking honestly in a safety review. I think that is true. A nurse who fears a transcript will not say what she saw at three in the morning.

But honestly, I am not a lawyer, and I have read subsection 6.2 four times and I still cannot tell you what it does in practice. What information could be withheld? From whom? What is the appeal? Nobody at the briefing could give me an example. That clause needs to be gone over line by line in committee.

The bill also widens disclosure of incident reports and improvement findings. Learning across the system is a good objective, so long as the patient's name never travels with it. My fear is that the reports go up and never come back down. The nurse who could prevent the next fall never reads them.

One word runs through this bill: administration. New committees. New reporting obligations. New procedure. Administration is not a bad thing in itself, but the growth in it has to be matched by clinical benefit. Every hour a clinician spends preparing a report is an hour not spent with a patient. The government has to show us that the paperwork buys better care. I have not seen that yet.

The bill lets the minister order a health care organization to carry out an improvement plan. Somebody has to be answerable, and I accept that. I am less sure the centre should decide for everyone. The Moncton Hospital, a clinic that opens two days a week, and a nursing home in Perth-Andover do not run the same shop, and a plan written in Fredericton may fit none of them. The minister should back the judgment of the people doing the work rather than stand in for it.

Subsection 6.2 troubles me most. It says that where the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act wins. That is a big legal step. Government members are cutting a hole in the main privacy law that covers public bodies. The minister says people speak more freely in a review when they know it stays in the room, and that is fair — a nurse will not describe what went wrong at three in the morning if she thinks it ends up in a newspaper. Still, you do not override a privacy statute without showing your work. What could be withheld? From whom? Who hears the appeal? Keep too much secret and the public stops trusting the review. Keep too little and nobody reports honestly. The committee should go through this clause line by line.

The bill also widens who may see incident reports and improvement findings. Hospitals should learn from each other. Nobody should learn a patient's name. My worry is that the reports climb to a director's inbox and never come back down to the nurse, the ward clerk, and the porter who could stop the next fall.

Then there is the paperwork. New committees. New reports to file. New forms. Forms are not evil, but they have to buy something for the patient. Every hour a clinician spends at a keyboard is an hour off the floor. The minister has to show us what that hour bought.

Madam Speaker, as New Brunswickers gather around their Christmas trees this year, they will be exchanging more than just presents. They will be swapping stories about how the Holt government has turned its promises into mere ornaments: sparkly, shiny and completely hollow. First there was the balanced budget promise. "Balanced." That was the word used in this House, and we were told it would be delivered with fanfare and a drumroll. Instead, what do we have? A deficit under the tree. It is not even the gift that keeps on giving. It is the gift that keeps on taking. Then there is the carbon tax adjustor. The member opposite has told this House more than once that it is complicated. It is not complicated. It is a promise so simple it could have been done with the stroke of a pen. This government needs to realize that promises are not just for the Christmas season. They are for the whole year. It is time they delivered.

Mr. Speaker, labour relations in this province are in bad shape, and that hurts everybody who is trying to build something here. This government's legislative approach has fallen short, and members ought to say so plainly. Going forward, ministers should sit down with workers and their representatives, tell them the truth and treat them decently. Nobody's interests get protected if the people on either side of that table do not trust each other.

Mr. Speaker, in December 2019 this Legislature fought over the essential service legislation, which was aimed squarely at the wages of nursing home workers. That was Bill 17. It imposed conditions on how labour arbitrators could rule on those wages, and it set off an intense reaction. Members of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions came out against it. They said it would hurt their ability to strike and their ability to negotiate a fair wage. They were loud about it, and they were loud because they were angry.

The bill passed. Union leaders called it an attack on public-sector labour unions, and they did not soften it. Sharon Teare, President of the New Brunswick Council of Nursing Home Unions, avowed that their voice would not be silenced. She said they would keep fighting for better working conditions and for the rights of nursing home workers, the people who bathe your mother, feed her and sit with her when nobody else can.

Bill 17 showed how much tension there is between this government and the labour unions in New Brunswick, on labour rights and on collective bargaining in particular. It showed how hard it is for a government to hold the interests of workers, the interests of taxpayers and its own books in the same hand.

And when we look back at December 2019 and the passage of Bill 17, we cannot forget who was standing where. There are members of this government today who opposed that bill. They said so out loud. They said they would stand with the labour movement as long as they could. That has changed today.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to recognize the enduring significance of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, fought on April 9, 1917, one of the defining moments in Canada's history. I am not a historian, and I will not pretend to know the tactics of that morning the way some members here do. What I know is the date and what it cost. Since 2006, the Vimy Foundation has been dedicated to raising awareness and educating Canadians about the battle. This year's campaign marks the beginning of the lead up to the 110th anniversary of the Battle of Vimy Ridge in 2027, a milestone moment in Canada's history. As we approach Vimy Week, from April 2 to 9, I encourage all members of this House to wear the Vimy Pin. Composed of four distinct colours, this pin symbolizes the unity and sacrifice of the four Canadian divisions that fought together for the first time at Vimy Ridge. I had to be told that, the first year I wore one. By wearing it, we honour their courage, their sacrifice and the legacy they left behind, a legacy that helped define our nation. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, on October 24 our community marked the 105th birthday of Ms. Laura Anderson, of Newtown. Laura is still in her own home, still living independently, and she is strong and vibrant. Until this past month she kept her driver's licence and took short drives out on the rural roads she knows better than the maps do. Laura and her late husband, Thomas, were founding members of the Agricultural Museum of New Brunswick. They were pioneers in agriculture and in tourism in this province, and the farming heritage they helped preserve is still there to be seen. In 1967, they opened New Brunswick's very first farm vacation. Families and travellers came from across the province and from around the world. Laura still has her humour and her stories. She has the wisdom too, and she will give it to you whether or not you asked for it. One hundred and five years. We thank her for what she has given this province. Happy birthday, Laura.

Madam Speaker, our government has tabled the 2026-27 capital budget, and it is a historic one: $1.47 billion, $200 million more than last year, the largest this province has ever tabled. Most of that money goes to the Department of Transportation and Infrastructure. It pays for roads, bridges, ferries and the other essential infrastructure New Brunswickers use without thinking about it. Hospitals get their share too — new medical equipment, and renovations to the buildings themselves. Shediac gets a new school. So does Moncton. Several other institutions around the province get upgrades. We did not invent this backlog. Governments underinvested for years, and someone has to pay that down. These investments keep people safe, they make life better here, and they leave our communities something to work with. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Moreover, the treatment of nursing home workers under Premier Higgs' leadership was concerning. I am not a labour lawyer, and I will not pretend I have read every clause of the arbitration changes. I have read enough. This government took nursing home workers to court and suggested that they relocate to Alberta for better wages. I do not know how anyone says that out loud to a woman who has spent 20 years lifting residents out of bed in Bathurst. It was a failure in negotiation and a betrayal of the people who provide essential care to our vulnerable populations. The 16-day school strike, and the emergency orders used to force workers back, raised questions about this government's commitment to meaningful dialogue and to the right to strike. Those measures undermined the very principles of a fair and balanced negotiation process. Watering down binding arbitration, introducing scab-friendly legislation, and this pension bill are a pattern that erodes the foundation of workers' rights. They do not align with the principles of a just and equitable society. It is our duty to scrutinize and question these policies, because the decisions made by government impact the livelihoods of countless individuals and the health of our communities. Madam Deputy Speaker, you will recall the unions expressing their vehement disagreement with the wage-freeze restriction mandate proposed by the Higgs government — the 0% wage mandate in the early years of this government. In the face of a global pandemic, our frontline workers were nothing short of heroes. Their commitment and sacrifices demanded acknowledgement and tangible support. The union leaders rightly asserted that these heroes deserved more than zeroes in their wage agreements.

Bill 40, An Act to Amend the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act, proposes significant amendments to legislation that already establishes a framework for reviewing and learning from patient safety incidents. The minister told this House that the amendments will improve how health care incidents are reviewed, "strengthen collaboration", enhance consistency, and improve transparency for patients and families. Those are worthy objectives, and no reasonable person would oppose a system that learns better and communicates better. Yet legislation is not judged by its intentions. It is judged by its consequences. Before we create new structures or grant new powers, we must ask what specific problem the bill is trying to address. The existing Act already provides a framework for patient safety reviews, so what has failed? Are incident reviews not occurring? Are lessons not being shared? Are patients not being informed? Are health authorities ignoring recommendations? I raised these at the briefing on the bill, and the answer I got back was that the changes would bring "consistency". Consistency with what? Legislative changes should follow demonstrated gaps, and the government has not presented clear data showing a systemic failure under the current law. Without that, we risk legislating in search of a problem. Diagnosis before treatment. The bill also creates the New Brunswick Quality of Care and Patient Safety Advisory Committee, established and maintained by the minister. On paper this sounds reasonable. Who could oppose expert advice on patient safety? Here is where prudence requires us to slow down. Health care professionals in this province already operate within Horizon Health Network, Vitalité Health Network, the professional regulatory colleges, accreditation bodies, internal quality review committees, and patient advocacy offices. Are we improving outcomes or adding bureaucracy? Front-line workers are already telling us they spend more of their time filling out forms instead of caring for patients. If this committee becomes another reporting layer without measurable improvement, we will have worsened the very system we set out to help.

The bill gives the minister the power to require health care organizations to put improvement plans in place. Accountability is fair enough. I will say up front that I am not a clinician. I have never run a hospital and I would not pretend to know how one is run from the inside. What I do know is that these organizations are not alike. An urban hospital, a rural facility, a community clinic and a long-term care home do not have the same staff or the same week, and a single plan imposed from the centre may not fit the place it lands. Last winter I sat with a nurse manager in my riding who was covering three vacancies herself and filing the same reports as a site with a full complement. Ministerial authority should support improvement rather than replace the judgment of people like her.

The part I keep going back to is subsection 6.2. If the Health Quality and Patient Safety Act conflicts with the Right to Information and Protection of Privacy Act, this Act prevails. That is a significant legal step. The government is writing an exception into one of the core privacy protections governing public institutions. Its argument is that confidentiality encourages open discussion during safety reviews, and honestly, I accept that. A doctor who thinks the transcript will end up public will not say the useful thing. Overriding existing privacy legislation still demands rigorous justification. I have read the clause three times and I still cannot tell you what could be withheld, from whom, or whether anyone can appeal. I don't know. Maybe the minister does, and can walk us through it in committee, because this clause deserves that kind of scrutiny. Too much secrecy undermines public trust. Too little discourages honest reporting.

The bill also expands the rules for disclosing incident reports and improvement findings. Learning across the system is worth having, so long as the patient's identity is protected. My fear is that the information travels upward into the bureaucracy and never reaches the practitioner who could stop the next one. It has to travel sideways too.

Then there is the administration itself: new committees, new reporting obligations, new procedural requirements. I am not against any of it in principle. But every hour spent preparing a report is an hour not spent with a patient, and I have not yet seen this government show me that the care gets better at the end of it.

This arose from a court ruling, a ruling of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. People do not really know this, but the Ontario Superior Court of Justice is a lower court. It is not the Supreme Court of Canada, as one of my colleagues on the other side said this morning. It was appealable. It was not a great decision, because this is already dealt with. Although it is not a law, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, and one of my colleagues on this side said that this is how it is dealt with currently, can actually deal with these lost Canadians very easily with her current power. She knows that. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, or IRCC, knows that, but the department will not admit it. That is the problem here. The government is doing something here, but it already has tools to address it, and it is widening the whole approach to this to make sure we are doing something. Most Canadians would say, “What are you doing, and why are you doing it?” Bill C-3, an act to amend the Citizenship Act, effectively says that we are opening the door here, for all intents and purposes, for the foreseeable future and confusing everybody, causing some problems that we are going to have to address one way or another. Canadian citizenship is not just a passport. It is a privilege, a responsibility and a bond to this country. Bill C-3 would weaken that bond. It would allow people with minimal ties to Canada to claim the same rights and benefits as those who have lived, worked and contributed here.

Mr. Speaker, let me say off the top that I will be splitting my time with a great new member, the hon. member for Terra Nova—The Peninsulas. Since this is my first time speaking for a substantive length of time since the election, please allow me to thank the hard-working, industrious people of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North for the honour of being their voice and their servant and for carrying their hopes and dreams to this place. While I have lived and worked in other places in North America in my career, I have always felt and known that the communities of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North are my true home, and home is where the heart is. It is the honour of my lifetime to serve these great communities. I want to thank my campaign team, including Simon, Mona, Jordan, Wendy, Jim and hundreds of volunteers. Above all, I thank my wife, Tracy, without whose love and support I certainly would not be here today. I will now go to the matter at hand. Canadians are struggling, not because we lack talent and not because we lack resources, but because we are too often being held back by red tape, gatekeeping and a government that over-promises and under-delivers. Nowhere is that clearer than when it comes to getting big projects built or trying to move goods and services and workers across provincial lines in our own country. These barriers do not cost us only time and money. They cost us opportunities, they cost us investments and they cost us jobs. That is why Bill C-5, an act to enact the free trade and labour mobility in Canada act and the building Canada act, is such a missed opportunity. It claims to deliver free trade and fast-tracked projects. What it would actually deliver is bureaucratic theatre, and a showpiece of announcements without the substance to back them up.

More than $220 million in federal funding, on the department's own announcements, went to Stellantis before it announced it was shifting production to the United States. At Algoma Steel, the Liberals approved loans of, I believe, about $400 million, even though they knew the company's business plan included major layoffs. They are literally subsidizing the loss of Canadian jobs. Folks who work in the auto industry, including those at Honda in my community of Alliston, know their livelihoods could be next, because if the government will not fight for workers in Brampton, Windsor, Oshawa or the Soo, it will not fight for them either. If the Liberals' failure to stand up to the United States was not bad enough, an equally serious and entirely self-inflicted threat to the Canadian auto industry comes from their own policies. Their obsessive push for an EV mandate has created uncertainty across the sector. For years, they have warned manufacturers and consumers that gas-powered vehicles would be banned, only to delay its implementation and repeatedly review and assess it. It has been delayed again, and there is still no clarity on what comes next. How can an industry that plans years in advance function when the Liberal government cannot provide even the most basic certainty? Automakers are finalizing their 2028 models today, and they are still guessing at what they will be able to manufacture under this shifting mandate. This has nothing to do with Donald Trump or the United States. The uncertainty choking the Canadian auto industry is made in Ottawa by the Liberals. They boast about supporting pipelines while key ministers work behind the scenes to stop them from ever being built. They scrapped the consumer carbon tax only to impose a harsher industrial version that lands squarely on manufacturers. With their shifting EV mandate, the same pattern repeats: big rhetoric about confronting Trump and strengthening the auto sector, even as they cripple the industry with policies that undermine its ability to survive. Auto workers deserve good, stable, paying jobs in a competitive climate that attracts investment.

While the Liberal government continues to rack up debt and deficits, cost of living pressures mount. There are higher taxes, higher inflation and a rising burden on ordinary Canadians. At the same time, we see record food bank growth, including in my constituency at the Samaritan House Ministries food bank in downtown Brandon. This is a rising burden on ordinary Canadians that is resulting in families skipping meals and seniors being forced to choose between heating their homes or putting fuel in their cars. That is not governmental success. It is a systemic failure on a grand scale, and it is forcing more and more Canadians to be reliant on government handouts just to get by. The Liberal answer is more government programs, more spending and more planning, increasing the money supply, raising debt and calling it investment. This does not change the reality that every dollar collected from Canadians is being poured into interest payments and debt service rather than helping Canadian families make ends meet. I find it ironic that after a decade of lecturing Canadians, the Liberals have finally admitted what Conservatives have said from the very beginning. The carbon tax was a costly, punishing failure, and the mental gymnastics that these Liberals now go through, after 10 years of flogging how the carbon tax was going to save the planet and then proudly putting forward a bill that cancelled it, are nothing short of hypocritical. For years they mocked and demonized anyone who questioned their tax-and-spend climate scheme, and they told families in southwestern Manitoba that paying more to heat their homes, drive their trucks and buy their groceries was somehow good for them in the long run. Now 10 years later, in the middle of an affordability crisis that they helped create, the Liberals are desperately trying to walk back the very policy that they flogged and pushed for countless years.

Madam Speaker, I rise at second reading of Bill C-19, and I will say at the outset that Conservatives will support it, because families need help right now. We will let the bill before us pass, because every dollar matters when families are choosing between groceries and other essentials. Before this goes to the Standing Committee on Finance, though, let us be honest about what it is. It is a band-aid solution that barely covers a few trips to the grocery store. This is a recycled Trudeau-era policy that would provide temporary relief without addressing the fundamental problem of driving grocery costs through the roof.

I have heard my colleague from Winnipeg North from across the way say that the Prime Minister is focused. He will keep saying that, and he will repeat it, but the Prime Minister is looking at life through a straw. He needs to take the straw away, open up his eyes and see the problems. The Liberals need to take the focus off trying to make themselves look good and focus on the root issues, the root problems that we are facing and that every household in Canada is facing.

We are supporting families in this crisis, but we refuse to pretend that the bill would fix anything. While the government offers handouts with one hand, its policies continue to drive up costs with the other. If it wants to be transparent, then disclose all the taxes that go into something. I remember doing that as the mayor of my city of Moose Jaw. In their tax roll, we showed everyone where their taxes were going. I raised that when the estimates were before committee in the fall, and I intend to raise it again at clause-by-clause on this bill. Our constituents should understand where their taxes go when they are going to the grocery store, and they should understand the costs that are being driven up by the Liberal government.

When a father in Deer Lake fills up his truck to go to work, he is paying a premium for the Liberal government's ideology. When a senior in Burgeo looks at the cost of home heating fuel, she is being squeezed by a Liberal plan that makes her life harder every single day. In that context, one would expect legislation from the Department of Finance to show restraint and focus on affordability. Instead, it introduces $37 billion in new Liberal spending, on top of tens of billions already committed. It proposes the creation of a sovereign wealth fund that has no wealth behind it, relying instead on borrowed money. It would allocate billions more to international climate finance, millions for conferences and billions in subsidies that would do little to address the immediate pressures facing hard-working Canadians. This is not a targeted plan to help families. It is an expansion of government at a time when Canadians need the exact opposite.

Liberals brag about $37 billion in spending. If we talk to the sort of small business owner the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, or CFIB, speaks for, or walk into any grocery store between Deer Lake and Burgeo and ask how they are managing to navigate in this environment, they do not want to hear about billions of dollars for international climate conferences. They want to know when prices are going to start to go down so they can manage to drive their kids to the activities they love and, at the same time, keep food on their tables. Seniors still living in their homes on a fixed income want to know when their money will once again be enough to live off. Entrepreneurs want to have confidence that they can grow their business and hire more staff instead of constantly facing more costs that create uncertainty and stress. They want to innovate and work on their business instead of constantly wondering how they are going to make payroll. When the estimates come before the Standing Committee on Finance, those are the questions I intend to put.

If we are talking about common sense, one of the things the Liberal government has forgotten is the Canadian winter. I am from the Prairies, and I can assure the House that winter is not just a season. It is a test of endurance. We might get March break, but it is a long season. It is endurance when we have -20°C days on a regular basis, -30°C for weeks at a time, and wind chills that blow snow across every single street and road. In these conditions, electric vehicles do not perform the way that they were advertised to, that they were supposed to. The battery range plummets, charging takes longer, running the heater or the defroster drains the power, and suddenly the EV becomes a liability when someone gets stuck in the middle of a gravel road on a dark, windy, storm-filled night.

Forgive me if I am a little skeptical when the government that is unable to introduce a budget tells me it has figured out this whole plan, this infrastructure plan and this EV mandate plan. It cannot even plant trees right. Do members remember the two billion trees the government was supposed to plant? It cannot even do that right, never mind get a network of EV chargers across this country.

I believe in innovation. I believe in technology. I believe in smart environmental policy. However, I also believe in freedom, something the Liberal government seems to have forgotten. I also believe in common sense, something the Liberal government has yet to come close to mastering. If EVs are the future, which they may be, they should not need government mandates to succeed. They should win on the open market by competing on cost and competing on performance and reliability. The mandate does none of that, and no one across the way has yet told me what happens to those advertised range figures on a -30°C morning in January.

This is a recurring theme with the Liberal government's approach to the economy. It is always our people who have to suffer the consequences of this Prime Minister's economic and trade failures, and right now they are struggling in record numbers. New insolvency data from the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy shows that over 37,000 Canadians filed for insolvency in the first quarter of 2026, which I believe is the highest level since the great recession. Statistics Canada has our people carrying about $2.6 trillion in household debt, and mortgage delinquency has reached its highest level in roughly five years. With this spring economic update, the Liberals are adding more debt, more costs and more taxes on the backs of Canadians, who are already at the breaking point.

Even worse, all this is taking place while Canada is still without a trade agreement with the United States. The uncertainty, tariffs and job losses that flow from that into auto manufacturing, into agriculture and right across the economy have more of an impact than anything announced in this update. The Liberals are failing on both fronts. They have not lowered the debt, increased investment or unleashed our economy, and they still have not gotten Canadians the trade deal they need.

The Liberals would have us believe that if one does not support their spending, their failures and their misplaced priorities, they somehow do not support this country. I find that argument crazy. Some members in this House may choose to set aside their principles to prop up this government. However, as a member of His Majesty's loyal opposition, my job is not to blindly support the government's agenda. My job is to make Canada the best it can be by holding the government to account on behalf of Canadians.

However, there is an even more troubling pattern here. Under the Canada–United Kingdom Trade Continuity Agreement, the U.K. has not been acting fairly toward our pork and cattle producers. The U.K. objects to carcass washes applied at Canadian slaughter plants and opposes the use of growth promotants in beef and pork production. The trade statistics tell the real story of the Liberal government's failure to stand up for our producers. Britain exported over 40 million dollars' worth of beef into Canada in 2024 and nearly 30 million dollars' worth in the first half of 2025. In comparison, Canada exported to Britain just 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024 and, to date, has no beef exports in 2025. For those who are watching, that is 25,000 dollars' worth in 2024, which is unbelievable. This is not fair trade. This is a one-way street that favours British producers, while our farmers and ranchers face non-tariff barriers designed to shut them down. The Canadian Cattle Association and the Canadian Pork Council have both put that on the record at the Standing Committee on International Trade.

As a mayor, I learned that economic development happens through work, not announcements. We attracted major investment to Moose Jaw by rolling up our sleeves and delivering results, $1.3 billion of results in six years, not by staging photo ops but by standing up for our community and for our businesses. The government has forgotten that lesson.

The U.K. and Canada share more than just a monarch. We share values, institutions and centuries of partnership. From Vimy Ridge to Afghanistan, we have stood together. Now, when it comes to trade, we are making them wait while we sort out our bureaucratic mess. During my time at King's College London, I witnessed Britain's commitment to innovation, enterprise and global engagement. The U.K.'s decision to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, or CPTPP, represents exactly that forward-thinking approach. Meanwhile, Canada is dragging its feet like we are still debating whether trade is good for the economy.

Madam Speaker, I rise on the opposition motion before the House today, the motion calling on the government to deliver immediate relief at the pump, and I will be splitting my time. A parent in my riding got up this morning, strapped their kids in the car and drove them to school. They then went to work. Before they did any of that, they stopped at the pump. One year ago, that fill-up cost them roughly $92 for a minivan. Last week, it cost them more than $127. Next week, it might be more. Over the years, deliberate policy choices the Liberal government has made built a tax structure on fuel that now squeezes Canadians every time they grip the nozzle. The Prime Minister says he wants to govern in a collaborative way, but the results are nonexistent, and it is time for his rhetoric to match reality. He is out to remove only one tax, the fuel excise tax, and only from April 20 until Labour Day, which is why the affordability promise is an illusion. The CAA's own price tracker tells the story plainly. Gas across Canada now averages more than $1.82 a litre, up from $1.32 a year ago and just $1.52 six weeks ago, a 38% spike in the cost of getting to work, getting kids to school and getting food to market. For millions of Canadians already living paycheque to paycheque, this compounding crisis, layered on top of crises the government has created, is too much to bear. Conservatives have brought a specific plan for relief at the pump, and we are calling on the government to adopt it. I raised the same numbers in question period three weeks ago and got no answer. Government members will rise today and tell us this is about global oil markets. They will reference the Middle East. They will explain the Strait of Hormuz. The Prime Minister used that exact description at a press conference, saying it is beyond Canada's control and asking what we could possibly do.

Madam Speaker, Canada has the expertise. We have the workers, we have the minerals, we have the manufacturing capacity and now we have the vision to be an energy superpower for the 21st century. Since 2020, over $34 billion has flowed to Canada through major investments in the batteries and automotive supply chain, and that is just the beginning. These investments are not distant promises. Factories are going up and equipment is coming in, and on top of that, developing new mines and new processing plants for a national EV supply chain will contribute upward of $16 billion to our annual GDP and create up to 40,000 well-paying jobs over the next decade for our children and our grandchildren. That is real economic growth with a real impact on real people's lives. To realize these benefits, Canada has been building. We know that making the decision to switch to electric vehicles is a big step for most families, and that is why we have invested in practical support. Canadians will benefit from a network of tens of thousands of electric vehicle chargers funded by the zero-emission vehicle infrastructure program, and with the Canada Infrastructure Bank deploying another 5,000 EV chargers, we are making sure charging is available for rural, remote and urban communities, so that range anxiety soon becomes a thing of the past. The electric vehicle availability standard that the Conservatives are opposing will actually incentivize the construction of thousands of new charging stations, and Canadians deserve real, reliable information about their options rather than what they have been hearing across the way. Over the past weekend I was at a shopping mall in my riding. There were half a dozen chargers there, and every one of them was filled with someone filling up their car, which happens very quickly. They would move out and someone else would move in. I counted four turnovers in the time it took me to have a coffee with a constituent who had driven in from Elmvale.

Madam Speaker, I rise to continue debate on Bill C-12 at second reading, and I want to pick up where I left off before question period. The failures do not end there. The Liberals also refuse to acknowledge their abject failure on border security, another critical element that Bill C-12 purportedly aims to address. Earlier this year, the Canada Border Services Agency revealed that 600 foreign criminals were scheduled for deportation, but now they have gone missing in custody. This is completely unacceptable and represents a grave threat to public safety. Canada's border must be secure to protect Canadians from criminals and illegal activities, including fentanyl trafficking and gun smuggling. Canadians deserve better from their government, one that respects their privacy, does not overreach with warrantless surveillance powers and is serious about fighting fentanyl by imposing real consequences on traffickers. Canadians deserve a government that protects our borders, enforces immigration laws fairly and firmly and supports law enforcement in combatting organized crime, and a government that does not leave foreign criminals at large in our communities. Canadians are looking to this House for leadership, not partisanship, on critical issues like public safety and immigration. Members will recall that this bill only exists because its predecessor, Bill C-2, was withdrawn after second reading collapsed on the government. While we have serious concerns about how the government first approached matters in that bill, we also acknowledge that Bill C-12 represents a step in the right direction. This very step came because Canadians raised their voices and the Conservatives did our job: We were listening, we pushed back and we demanded better on behalf of the citizens of this country. Our work here is not done. We will support sending Bill C-12 to the Standing Committee on Public Safety and National Security, where it will be scrutinized carefully clause by clause, and where I expect the agency to be asked directly, on the record, what became of those 600 deportation files.

Madam Speaker, when it comes to housing, bureaucrats count starts. They count units. They count dollars. They count funds, programs, agencies and promises, but in Nanaimo—Ladysmith, we count something different. We count the months our adult children have been living in the spare room because rent has eaten the down payment they were trying to save for. We count the number of graduates who cannot find a job that pays enough to cover rent. We count the number of people with no home at all as we pass them on the way to work. Before I forget, I will be splitting my time. On a more serious note, we count the graves of friends lost to addiction, the treatment beds that are not there, and the people who make it through detox only to be sent back to the same chaos they were trying to escape. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation reports starts. My constituents report the gap between the government's language and their own week. A young person in Cedar finished a diploma last spring, found a job and still has no real path to owning a home in the community she grew up in. A man discharged from a detox bed in Nanaimo in March went into the only unit Island Health could place him in, with drug use going on down the hall, and he lasted eleven days. Those two files sit in the same constituency office folder, because the same failure of government produced them. We have lost the link between housing and hope. Canada does not lack for housing announcements. In the last decade, governments have rolled out strategies, accelerators, funds, agencies, accords and photo ops, including some that have their own complete purpose-built backdrop. What we do not have is enough homes that people can afford. In Nanaimo—Ladysmith, we do not have enough of the right homes for people who are trying to rebuild their lives.

Building a stronger Canada takes government, industry and world-class polytechnic institutions. In Burnaby Central, we are proud to be home to the British Columbia Institute of Technology, a national leader defining what polytechnic education means in Canada. BCIT is more than a school. It is where Canada's welders, electricians, engineers, technicians, nurses and innovators get the hands-on training that builds our country and infrastructure, powers our industries and strengthens our economy. As our government advances $115.2 billion in infrastructure investment, we will rely on BCIT more than ever, because without skilled apprentices, trained tradespeople and innovators ready to lead, no major project gets built, not on time and not on budget. BCIT is building the workforce of tomorrow, and our job is to make sure institutions like BCIT have the tools to keep doing that. I do not think we have finished that job. Innovation is happening in Burnaby too. I recently toured three remarkable companies. Novarc Technologies is a global leader in welding automation, using AI robotics to tackle complex industrial applications, which is critical as Canada ramps up infrastructure and clean technology projects. Svante Technologies is a world leader in carbon capture, turning climate ambition into action and helping Canada lead in clean technology. BlueForce Energy advances the low-carbon transition through electric fleet conversions, battery storage and renewable energy solutions. To compete globally, Canada must reduce its carbon intensity. In Burnaby, leading innovators are showing how Canadian expertise, from advanced manufacturing to clean technology, can drive a cleaner, stronger and more competitive future. Emma reminded me that young Canadians already understand one important truth: we cannot rely on one trading partner. Seventy per cent of our exports go to the United States, so trade diversification is essential, and I will admit I did not have a good answer for Emma when she asked me which markets take up that share, or how long that would take us.

This arose from a court ruling, a superior court ruling in Ontario. People do not really know this, but a superior court is a lower court. It is not the Supreme Court, as one of my colleagues on the other side said this morning. It was appealable. It was not a great decision, because this is already dealt with. Although it is not a law, there is a process by which the Minister of Immigration, and one of my colleagues on this side said that this is how it is dealt with currently, can actually deal with these lost Canadians very easily with her current power. She knows that. The government knows that, but it will not admit it. Canadian citizenship is not just a passport. It is a privilege, a responsibility and a bond to this country. Bill C-3 would weaken that bond, because it would allow people with minimal ties to Canada to claim the same rights and benefits as those who have lived, worked and contributed here. That is the problem here. The government is doing something when it already has tools to address it, and it is widening the whole approach to this to make sure we are doing something. Most Canadians would say, “What are you doing, and why are you doing it?” It effectively says that we are opening the door here, for all intents and purposes, for the foreseeable future and confusing everybody, causing problems we are going to have to address one way or another. When the bill reaches committee, I want the department to tell us, case by case, how many grants the minister has already made under the authority she has now and how many files are still sitting in the queue. I asked for that figure before the election and I have not been given it yet, so I am not willing to take on faith the claim that the existing authority cannot do the job.

Under the Liberal government, there is a two-tier tax code for Canadians. There is one for the rich Liberal friends of the Prime Minister and another for everyone else. Worse yet, in this costly Liberal budget, the Liberal Prime Minister gave himself and his buddies a tax break on the purchase of luxury yachts and private jets, while voting against scrapping taxes on food and groceries. The Liberal Prime Minister helped design a tax system he did not have to live under because he was living outside of it. While Brookfield was safely storing profits in Bermuda, small charities and family businesses faced the full force of the Liberal tax-collecting agency. On top of egregious tax avoidance, the Liberal Prime Minister's conflict of interest cover-up is even worse. Brookfield's chief operating officer was asked about the screen this month, and this is what he said: “The screen applies to a defined list of entities. I can confirm that approximately 95 per cent of the companies in the portfolio are not on that list. Those companies are managed independently of the individual and, in our view, they are not captured by the arrangement as it was filed.” Those are not the opposition's words. That means 1,900 companies stand to benefit from government decisions that will enrich the Prime Minister personally at the expense of taxpayers, and Canadians will be kept in the dark about how those companies are involved. The Liberal Prime Minister is even taking private meetings with Brookfield executives at the Prime Minister's Office and while he travels overseas. With ethics like this, how can Canadians trust him? He is starting to look a lot like the last Liberal prime minister, just more costly. At the end of the day, Canadians deserve a prime minister whose loyalty is to the public, not to his private portfolio or the shareholders of Brookfield.

Mr. Speaker, let me say off the top that I will be splitting my time with a great new member, the hon. member for Terra Nova—The Peninsulas. Since this is my first time speaking for a substantive length of time since the election, please allow me to thank the hard-working, industrious people of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North for the honour of being their voice and their servant and for carrying their hopes and dreams to this place. While I have lived and worked in other places in North America in my career, I have always felt and known that the communities of Flamborough—Glanbrook—Brant North are my true home, and home is where the heart is. It is the honour of my lifetime to serve these great communities. I want to thank my campaign team, including Simon, Mona, Jordan, Wendy, Jim and hundreds of volunteers. Above all, I thank my wife, Tracy, without whose love and support I certainly would not be here today. I will now go to the matter at hand. Canadians are struggling, not because we lack talent and not because we lack resources, but because we are too often being held back by red tape, gatekeeping and a government that over-promises and under-delivers. Nowhere is that clearer than when it comes to getting big projects built or trying to move goods and services and workers across provincial lines in our own country. These barriers do not cost us only time and money. They also cost us opportunities, investments and jobs. That is why Bill C-5, an act to enact the free trade and labour mobility in Canada act and the building Canada act, is such a missed opportunity. It claims to deliver free trade and fast-tracked projects, but the reality is that it would deliver bureaucratic theatre, a showpiece of announcements without the substance to back them up.

More than $220 million in federal funding went to Stellantis before it announced it was shifting production to the United States, and at Algoma Steel the Liberals approved $400 million in loans, even though they knew the company's business plan included major layoffs. They are literally subsidizing the loss of Canadian jobs. The workers in Brampton were told the money would keep the line running. The workers in Windsor were told the money would keep the line running. The workers in the Soo were told the money would keep the line running. Folks who work in the auto industry, including those at Honda in my community of Alliston, know their livelihoods could be next, because if the government will not fight for workers in Oshawa, it will not fight for them either. If the Liberals' failure to stand up to the United States was not bad enough, an equally serious and entirely self-inflicted threat to the Canadian auto industry comes from their own policies. Their obsessive push for an EV mandate has created uncertainty across the sector. For years, they have warned manufacturers and consumers that gas-powered vehicles would be banned, only to delay its implementation and repeatedly review and assess it. It has been delayed again, and there is still no clarity on what comes next. How can an industry that plans years in advance function when the Liberal government cannot provide even the most basic certainty? Automakers are finalizing their 2028 models today, but they are still guessing at what they will be able to manufacture under this shifting mandate. This has nothing to do with Donald Trump or the United States. The uncertainty choking the Canadian auto industry is made in Ottawa by the Liberals. They boast about supporting pipelines while key ministers work behind the scenes to stop them from ever being built. They scrapped the consumer carbon tax only to impose a harsher industrial version that lands squarely on manufacturers. With their shifting EV mandate, the same pattern repeats. Auto workers deserve good, stable, paying jobs in a competitive climate that attracts investment.

Madam Speaker, I rise at second reading of the budget implementation bill on behalf of the people of Brandon—Souris. While the Liberal government continues to rack up debt and deficits, cost of living pressures mount. There are higher taxes, higher inflation and a rising burden on ordinary Canadians. At the same time, we see record food bank growth, including in my constituency at the Samaritan House Ministries food bank in downtown Brandon. This is a rising burden on ordinary Canadians that is resulting in families skipping meals and seniors being forced to choose between heating their homes or putting fuel in their cars. That is not governmental success. It is a systemic failure on a grand scale that is forcing more and more Canadians to be reliant on government handouts just to get by. The Liberal answer is more government programs, more spending and more planning, increasing the money supply, raising debt and calling it investment. This does not change the reality that every dollar collected from Canadians is being poured into interest payments and debt service rather than helping Canadian families make ends meet. When officials appeared at the finance committee last week, not one of them could tell us what the debt service line will be in three years. I find it ironic that after a decade of lecturing Canadians, the Liberals have finally admitted what Conservatives have said from the very beginning. The carbon tax was a costly, punishing failure, and the mental gymnastics that these Liberals now go through, after 10 years of flogging how the carbon tax was going to save the planet and then proudly putting forward a bill that cancelled it, are nothing short of hypocritical. For years they mocked and demonized anyone who questioned their tax-and-spend climate scheme, and they told families in southwestern Manitoba that paying more to heat their homes, drive their trucks and buy their groceries was somehow good for them in the long run. Now 10 years later, in the middle of an affordability crisis that they helped create, the Liberals are desperately trying to walk back the very policy that they flogged and pushed for countless years.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at the second reading stage of Bill C-19, and let me say at the outset that Conservatives will support it, because families need help right now. We will let the bill before us pass, because every dollar matters when families are choosing between groceries and other essentials. However, let us be honest about what this is. It is a band-aid solution that barely covers a few trips to the grocery store. This is a recycled Trudeau-era policy that would provide temporary relief without addressing the fundamental problem of driving grocery costs through the roof. I have heard my colleague from Winnipeg North from across the way say, in this debate and in the one before it, that the Prime Minister is focused. He will keep saying that, and he will repeat it, but the Prime Minister is looking at life through a straw. He needs to take the straw away, open up his eyes and see the problems. The Liberals need to take the focus off trying to make themselves look good and focus on the root issues, the root problems that we are facing and that every household in Canada is facing. We are supporting families in this crisis, but we refuse to pretend that the bill would fix anything. While the government offers handouts with one hand, its policies continue to drive up costs with the other. When this bill reaches the Standing Committee on Finance, I hope members will put the transparency question to the officials directly. If the government wants to be transparent, then disclose all the taxes that go into something. I remember doing that as the mayor of my city of Moose Jaw. In their tax roll, we showed everyone where their taxes were going, and we should be able to do that for the constituents of our ridings when they are going to the grocery store. They should understand where their taxes go so that they understand the costs that are being driven up by the Liberal government.

When a father in Deer Lake fills up his truck to go to work, he is paying a premium for the Liberal government's ideology. When a senior in Burgeo looks at the cost of home heating fuel, she is being squeezed by a Liberal plan that makes her life harder every single day. In that context, one would expect the legislation to show restraint and focus on affordability, but instead, it introduces $37 billion in new Liberal spending, on top of tens of billions already committed. It proposes the creation of a sovereign wealth fund that has no wealth behind it, relying instead on borrowed money. It would allocate billions more to international climate finance, millions for conferences and billions in subsidies that would do little to address the immediate pressures facing hard-working Canadians. That is an expansion of government at a time when Canadians need the exact opposite, rather than a targeted plan to help families. Liberals brag about $37 billion in spending, yet if we talk to any small business owner or walk into any grocery store and ask how they are managing to navigate in this environment, they do not want to hear about billions of dollars for international climate conferences. They want to know when prices are going to start to go down so they can manage to drive their kids to the activities they love and, at the same time, keep food on their tables. Seniors still living in their homes on a fixed income want to know when their money will once again be enough to live off. Entrepreneurs want to have confidence that they can grow their business and hire more staff instead of constantly facing more costs that create uncertainty and stress. They want to innovate and work on their business instead of constantly wondering how they are going to make payroll. They want to continue to contribute to their communities instead of having to cut back because of constantly higher costs. I asked the minister about the heating fuel line in this bill during questions and comments last week, and I have not had an answer yet.

If we are talking about common sense, one of the things the Liberal government has forgotten is the Canadian winter. I am from the Prairies, and I can assure the House that winter is not just a season. It is a test of endurance. We might get March break, but it is a long season. It is endurance when we have -20°C days on a regular basis, -30°C for weeks at a time, and wind chills that blow snow across every single street and road. In these conditions, electric vehicles do not perform the way that they were advertised to, that they were supposed to. The battery range plummets, charging takes longer, running the heater or the defroster drains the power, and suddenly the EV becomes a liability when someone gets stuck in the middle of a gravel road on a dark, windy, storm-filled night. Forgive me if I am a little skeptical when the government that is unable to introduce a budget tells me it has figured out this whole plan, this infrastructure plan and this EV mandate plan. It cannot even plant trees right. Do members remember the two billion trees the government was supposed to plant? It cannot even do that right, never mind get a network of EV chargers across this country. I believe in innovation. I believe in technology. I believe in smart environmental policy. However, I also believe in freedom, something the Liberal government seems to have forgotten. I also believe in common sense, something the Liberal government has yet to come close to mastering. If EVs are the future, which they may be, they should not need government mandates to succeed. They should win on the open market by competing on cost and competing on performance and reliability. Before the mandate takes another step, I would like the minister to tell the House how many chargers are actually operating on the Prairies today and how many of them have been tested at -30°C. I have asked that question twice now and I still do not have the number.
